- **Selected pathway:** A, revised to include the proposed twenty-minute cue-focused opportunity instead of an assumed next harder stage.
- **Trajectory so far:** initial independent miss, helped grouping and correction; then A's learning attempts, explanation and four recorded fresh responses. Sixty minutes of the selected allocation have occurred. The new twenty-minute opportunity has not yet occurred.

The case shows model and plan revision without claiming that the revision itself changed N24. The new-context responses are local evidence; broader transfer, delayed retention and causal programme effectiveness remain separate questions.

#### HCD.6:5.7 - Preparing to Understand a Weighted Mean

This constructed lesson prepares a service coordinator to report mean active processing time per request from batch summaries. It supports a descriptive work report; predicting queue clearance would need other information. The coordinator can count requests, add durations, multiply and divide. On an entry task they correctly average individual request times, but average two batch means without considering how many requests each batch contains. The missing relation is each batch's contribution to the total across requests. A calculator, paper and a trainer competent in this arithmetic are available.

**Select contrasts from that relation.** In the supplied teaching data every request in a batch takes its stated active time. There is no waiting time to interpret and no missing request. The learner receives these inputs:

| Case | Batch with 10 minutes per request | Batch with 20 minutes per request |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E | 5 requests | 5 requests |
| A | 2 requests | 8 requests |
| B | 8 requests | 2 requests |
| C | 4 requests | 16 requests |

The designer's separate answer key gives E = 150 / 10 = 15, A = 180 / 10 = 18, B = 120 / 10 = 12 and C = 360 / 20 = 18 minutes per request. E makes the simple average of the two batch means plausible. A and B expose the importance of the mixture while keeping batch times and total request count unchanged. A and C change total size while preserving the mixture and the mean. Keep this key out of the initial learner sheet.

**Preparation through construction.** Ask: “Devise one calculation for the mean active minutes per request that works for all four cases. Show how it treats every request. Test it on another case before settling on it.” The learner may expand a batch into individual durations, draw groups or use arithmetic. Suppose their first rule is `(10 + 20) / 2 = 15`. It works for E. Ask them to test A by totaling its individual durations with operations they already know. The resulting 180 minutes across ten requests conflicts with the 150 minutes implied by their proposed mean. They now have a concrete question about the missing request counts. Have them test B and C with the same proposed rule or its revision. The trainer may clarify data and invite a comparison, recording help that supplies the missing relation. The learner need not derive a polished formula before the explanation begins.

**Preparation through a worked solution.** For the alternative, give the complete reasoning for A: two requests contribute `2 × 10 = 20` minutes; eight contribute `8 × 20 = 160`; divide their combined 180 minutes by all ten requests to obtain 18. Ask the learner to explain why each multiplier and the divisor are present, why 15 fails, what changes in B and why doubling both counts in C leaves the mean unchanged. They must use the data and explain the reasoning; copying 18 does not complete the preparation. An incorrect explanation identifies what the trainer should address next.

**Connect either preparation to the same explanation.** The trainer now explains that a batch's mean time `t`, multiplied by its request count `n`, supplies that batch's total active time. Across batches, `mean time per request = sum(n × t) / sum(n)`. Giving each batch equal weight answers a different question; for these two batch times it gives the per-request mean only when their counts are equal. The learner marks the counts, totals and final divisor in their own attempted or supplied solution, then uses the explanation to account for A versus B and A versus C. This gives the formula a relation to inspect instead of leaving the learner to memorize its symbols. If the learner already constructed the correct rule, use the explanation to make that connection explicit and move on.

**Use the relation in a new report.** The first fresh task has four requests at eight minutes each and six at eighteen: `(4 × 8 + 6 × 18) / 10 = 14` minutes per request. The learner supplies the calculation and its units. A second report changes the representation: eight requests have a batch total of 72 minutes, and two have a batch total of 28. The mean is `(72 + 28) / 10 = 10`; multiplying these totals by the counts again would count the work repeatedly. The learner must identify what the columns contain before calculating. During these attempts the explanation sheet and calculator remain available; the trainer gives no decisive prompt before recording the first response. Feedback then addresses the actual error, and correction may reuse that case.

The lesson returns the preparation response, the first responses after explanation, help received, correction and remaining difficulty. These observations can guide the next lesson. Success with the sheet is performance with that support. It does not by itself show improvement caused by preparation, independent transfer or retention. A comparison of preparations would need HCD.12:4.5's comparable conditions and actual observations; the arithmetic key supplies none.

**Make the choice fit the people and resources.** Both designs have a 40-minute learner allowance and a 45-minute provider allowance. The trainer can prepare beforehand and attend the stated contact periods. Materials and calculator access are available. The allocations below include preparing and checking the case sheets, common explanation and response criteria:

| Contribution | Construction preparation | Worked-solution preparation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider preparation before the lesson | 12 minutes | 14 minutes, including the worked reasoning |
| Learner preparation with trainer present | 10 minutes learner and 10 provider | 8 minutes learner and 8 provider |
| Common explanation and connection to the preparation | 8 minutes learner and 8 provider | 8 minutes learner and 8 provider |
| Fresh reports before feedback | 10 minutes learner; no provider contact | 10 minutes learner; no provider contact |
| Feedback and correction | 6 minutes learner and 6 provider | 6 minutes learner and 6 provider |
| Record the response and next need | 2 minutes learner and 2 provider | 2 minutes learner and 2 provider |
| Total allocated | 36 minutes learner; 38 provider | 34 minutes learner; 38 provider |

These are local planning allowances to test, not research-established doses. The small, fully supplied arithmetic cases make both preparations feasible proposals. Choose construction when entry evidence shows that the learner can generate and compare approaches and the useful question is which relation their approach overlooks. Choose the worked solution when constructing a method consumes the available attention but the learner can follow its steps and explain contrasts. This choice concerns fit, not a demonstrated superiority of either preparation.

For example, a second learner can explain the worked multipliers but cannot organize a calculation from the blank sheet: use the worked preparation and inspect their explanation before proceeding. If a learner already weights the cases and interprets batch totals reliably, omit both preparations and use practice for the remaining target. If qualified explanation or feedback is unavailable, restore that contribution through HCD.7/.8 or redesign within the actual resources. If the construction allowance is exhausted, do not append the entire worked route to it under the original totals; revise the remaining lesson or arrange another window.

### HCD.6:6 - Bias-Annotation


Lenses: **Gov**, **Arch**, **Onto/Epist**, **Prag**, **Did**. Scope: representative practice-task design for a named human contribution or an explicitly conditional future-audience branch.

| Recurring bias | Likely drift | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| surface-realism bias | A workplace story or visual detail is treated as representation. | Preserve the relations and conditions that elicit and discriminate the target action. |
| difficulty bias | More complexity is assumed to create more learning. | Remove irrelevant burden and vary only what changes the Method, action, or interpretation. |
| cue blindness | Method names, intermediate prompts, or AI output supply the answer being tested. | Declare permitted help; remove the answer-bearing cue when the attempt must elicit that contribution independently. |
| tool-removal bias | All references and tools are removed in the name of independence. | Retain legitimate later-Work supports and isolate only the human contribution the current task targets. |
| caution bias | Refusal is accepted in every uncertain case. | Include sufficient-evidence cases that require bounded action as well as genuine missing-evidence stops. |
| answer-key bias | The final answer is checked while the reasoning, source applicability, or critical error remains hidden. | Require the decision-bearing intermediate action and use domain criteria. |
| production-copy bias | A real case is copied without controlling risk, access, or confounding contributions. | Build a sufficiently whole bounded task and return professional facts to qualified owners. |
| assessment leakage | A supported or corrected practice attempt is reported as independent capability. | State each task's evidence purpose and preserve help and contamination history. |

### HCD.6:7 - Conformance Checklist

- [ ] The human holder or future-audience branch, later-Work family, target action, selected Method, practice purpose, and receiving use are explicit.
- [ ] A qualified target-domain source or stipulated teaching oracle supplies facts, calculations, result criteria, critical errors, hazards, and specialist boundaries.
- [ ] The task is sufficiently whole for the target action but omits complexity that changes neither action nor interpretation.
- [ ] The result recipient, decision or operation, required work product, and next move are visible.
- [ ] Human, reference, tool, AI, peer, teacher, specialist, environment, permission, and authority contributions remain distinct.
- [ ] Permitted help is stated before each attempt, and answer-bearing cues are removed only where the target requires it.
- [ ] Demonstrations and worked explanations expose the action or reasoning the learner needs; the practice set provides an opportunity to observe use of that help.
- [ ] Help and repetition fit the current practice purpose. When recognition, selection or adaptation is the target, the set includes a condition change that can expose that contribution.
- [ ] The set includes warranted refusal and supported continuation when that distinction belongs to the target.
- [ ] Feedback names the affected criterion and next action. Same-case correction is distinguished from a later changed-case observation of recognition or adaptation.
- [ ] Learner and provider resources include task, feedback, correction, and retry; an oversized case returns for redesign.
- [ ] The result states progression or return conditions and distinguishes demonstration, supported practice, independent practice, correction, transfer, retention, and effectiveness uses.
- [ ] Where a qualitative transition is proposed, its starting evidence, intended change, activity, allocated help, mechanism and discriminating observation are connected; a level label alone does not design practice.
- [ ] Any serious alternative pathway has entry and resource grounds. The model, selected plan and recorded trajectory stay distinct, including after an observation changes the model.

### HCD.6:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Change the pump to a ticket queue” | New nouns can preserve the same cue and answer. | Change a relation or condition that alters the warranted Method or result. |
| “Use a real project” | Production realism can add uncontrolled risk, access limits, and other human or specialist contributions. | Bound the task around the target action and obtain qualified domain and safety inputs. |
| “Repeating the shown answer demonstrates adaptation” | The repeated answer may depend on memory of that case. | Keep its legitimate practice use; test adaptation through a changed condition without supplying the answer being judged. |
| “No help means independent” | Removing legitimate references or tools can test a different contribution from later Work. | Specify the exact human contribution and retain compatible support conditions. |
| “Always refuse if evidence is uncertain” | Generic caution fails when sufficient compatible evidence supports bounded action. | Pair missing-evidence and sufficient-evidence variants with explicit criteria. |
| “The learner got it after feedback” | Corrected practice is contaminated by the feedback event. | Record help and test the affected action on a changed task before stronger inference. |
| “Harder is more representative” | Difficulty without target relevance raises burden and obscures the result. | Scale complexity to current knowledge and the action being elicited. |
| “The answer key defines professional truth” | An invented key can encode unsafe or wrong domain guidance. | Obtain a qualified domain source or label stipulated teaching facts and their limits. |

### HCD.6:9 - Consequences

The practitioner gains tasks that make a selected human action observable and correctable without pretending to be full production Work. Meaningful variations expose applicability, source compatibility, resource limits, and the difference between warranted refusal and supported continuation.

The cost is domain and provider work. Someone must qualify the facts and hazards, prepare cases, arrange any demonstrations or explanations the learner needs, review attempts, and prepare the variations needed to distinguish recognition or adaptation from answer recall. A task may return unfinished when correctness, access, safe conditions, or feedback capacity is absent.

### HCD.6:10 - Rationale

A practice task is representative relative to the target contribution and intended evidence claim. It preserves the relations needed for that contribution and use, not every detail of the workplace. This permits bounded safe practice while protecting domain truth.

Supported acquisition and correction can use the same task; a changed-condition attempt answers a different question when recognition or adaptation is required. Separating those uses keeps the learning contribution of help visible while preserving the limits of the resulting evidence. Designing both refusal and continuation cases prevents a safety-oriented boundary from becoming inert caution. The resulting work products give HCD.9 a focused practice object and HCD.11 an interpretable attempt without making their later conclusions in advance.

### HCD.6:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The working question is: **How should a practitioner design practice tasks that elicit a target human contribution and support meaningful correction and variation without mistaking surface realism for representation?**

The selected best-known line combines sufficiently whole complex tasks, expertise-sensitive worked support, and decision-bearing variation. The maintained [4C/ID model](https://www.4cid.org/about/) and its [fourth-edition presentation](https://www.4cid.org/readings/books/) supply the serious whole-task design candidate: learning tasks, support for non-routine reasoning, timely procedural information, and additional practice for recurrent parts. Paas and van Merriënboer's 2020 review ([`COG-05`](https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721420922183)) supports worked examples and integrated information for novices while warning that unchanged guidance can become redundant as task knowledge grows. HCD.6 adapts these contributions into §§4.2–4.3 and the separation of whole-task and focused-part practice. The amount of help and the use of a repeated or varied task follow the learning purpose and starting capability; the sources do not prescribe a changed condition for every correction.

The serious ordinary alternative is a topic exercise or surface-isomorphic scenario: present the rule, vary the nouns and numbers, and score the final answer. It is cheaper to produce, but it can preserve answer-bearing cues, omit the later-Work purpose and interfaces, and reward either calculation without judgement or generic caution. HCD.6 rejects surface change as representation and adds the decision-bearing variation, human/support allocation, domain criteria, and correction task in §§4.1–4.6.

Brunmair and Richter's 2019 meta-analysis ([`COG-03`](https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209)) supplies limit evidence that interleaving varies by material and similarity; it does not prescribe one mixed task set. Czyż, Wójcik, and Solarská's 2024 motor-learning review ([`COG-04`](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1377122)) supports testing delayed transfer while its applied estimate and cross-domain reach remain weak. Bastani and colleagues' 2025 school-mathematics trial ([`AI-04`](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122)) supports separating assisted practice from a later unassisted attempt; it does not supply an adult engineering effect or a universal AI ban. These sources change the task contrasts and evidence-purpose boundary rather than selecting one universal schedule.

The selected line costs more domain and case-design effort than renaming exercises, but it preserves action interpretability, legitimate support, critical errors, and the opportunity to learn from a changed result. Reopen it when stronger sources alter the whole-task, worked-support, variation, AI-help, or transfer boundary, or when representative use shows a lower-effort task design that preserves the same decision-bearing relations and evidence value.

For constructing a pathway from a qualitative model, [van Merriënboer's 4C/ID overview (2019)](https://www.4cid.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/vanmerrienboer-4cid-overview-of-main-design-principles-2021.pdf) supplies a developed comparison: task classes organize increasing complexity, with guidance reduced within a class and renewed when a harder class begins. HCD.6 adapts that design distinction in §4.2.1; a class of tasks is not a developmental state. [Expanded evidence-centered design](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00853) supplies the complementary connection from a proposed proficiency change to task support and observations. It does not establish which route works for N24. Compared with simply increasing difficulty after success, the construction exposes why a task and help might change the targeted response and what would redirect them. The additional preparation is warranted when that distinction changes the next learning opportunity; ordinary same-case correction still needs no complete progression model.

For preparation before a new explanation, [Schwartz's *Achieving an adaptive learner* (online 2024)](https://aaalab.stanford.edu/assets/papers/2024/achieving_an_adaptive_learner.pdf) develops the construction of a common account across chosen contrasts. It informs §4.2.2. The paper reinterprets earlier studies in selected STEM settings; broader generality and the joint necessity of its design principles remain unresolved. Its practical timing is not a universal dose. §5.7 is a constructed adaptation. Prompted explanation of a worked solution remains a serious alternative, supported by the expertise-sensitive guidance discussed above. Choose from entry evidence and complete resource demands, and reopen the choice when observations or stronger comparative evidence change it.

The historical [dance-marking study by Warburton and colleagues (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613478824) supplies a revealing comparison for §4.2.3: prepared ballet students used reduced movements while practising already learned steps, with improvement in subsequent overall expressive performance. This supports considering a simplified whole alongside full execution. It does not prescribe reduced effort for all novices or establish improvement on every performance measure. MDPE.10 supplies the subject-specific comparison of perception, execution and coordination; the teacher must preserve the relation that the reduction is meant to develop.

### HCD.6:12 - Relations


- **`HCD.1`, `HCD.3`, and `HCD.4`:** can supply the later-Work demand, qualified target, current evidence, protected strengths, and priority conditions. HCD.4:4.2.1–4.3.1 also constructs and tests a local qualitative model when the pathway needs it.
- **`HCD.2`:** can expose a programme component and task closure needing elaboration; HCD.6 does not select the programme.
- **`HCD.5`:** supplies the selected development Method, proposed mechanism, learner/task fit, support need, and evidence plan.
- **`HCD.7`:** establishes whether the required provider, source, tool, AI, access, environment, and human-check contributions are available.
- **`HCD.8`:** builds a missing task-production, provider, assessment, or practice-environment capability only when the required result is explicit.
- **`HCD.9`:** enacts the tasks, feedback, correction, and retries while recording the practice history.
- **`HCD.10`:** selects variation, spacing, interleaving, progression, or support change across practice episodes; HCD.6 supplies the meaningful task conditions.
- **`HCD.11`–`HCD.13`:** interpret condition-qualified performance, transfer, retention, and tool dependence; a task design or answer key is not those observations. HCD.12:4.5 also separates application after a new explanation from any causal contribution of the preceding preparation.
- **`HCD.14`:** distinguishes a changed learner position, a revised proficiency model and a revised learning arrangement, and can change the affected task, criterion, help or progression condition from compatible evidence.
- **LG.05 and other learning-product practices:** can explain and package a selected task; pedagogical presentation does not select the target relation or establish professional correctness.
- **Target-domain, safety, clinical, legal, employment, provider, privacy, and specialist practices:** retain correctness, hazard, participation, authority, and consequence decisions.

### HCD.6:End

## HCD.6.1 - Help a Learner Discern a Needed Distinction in Practice

> **Type:** Method pattern
> **Status:** Stable
> **Normativity:** Normative unless marked informative

### HCD.6.1:1 - Problem frame

Use this method when a learner can hear a term or follow a direction but cannot yet notice the difference on which the action depends. “Listen to the release,” “notice the waiting time” or “use the other method when this relation changes” may be meaningful to the teacher while leaving the learner without something they can recognize.

Construct an encounter in which that difference becomes accessible. Help the learner attend to it, use it and recognize it when incidental features or support change. The first result is a practice task and a learner response that can guide the next attempt. Learning, retention and transfer require observations suited to those further claims.

The target distinction must come from the relevant practice. If the teacher cannot yet explain or demonstrate it, recover that subject contribution first. If the learner already notices it reliably but cannot perform the required action, address that action or its coordination rather than repeat recognition exercises.

### HCD.6.1:2 - Problem

An expert has learned to pick out features that a novice does not notice. Naming the feature can help direct attention only after the learner has some way to recognize what the name refers to. More explanation in the same terms can leave this circularity intact.

Practice can also teach a misleading cue. A learner may associate the teacher's gesture, a color or the order of the examples with the answer, while the relation needed in later work remains unnoticed. Even a useful exercise can then fail to transfer.

### HCD.6.1:3 - Forces

| Need | Difficulty |
| --- | --- |
| Make the relevant feature accessible | Too many simultaneous differences can conceal what matters. |
| Preserve the intended work | A highly simplified exercise can remove the relation the learner must eventually use. |
| Begin with available capability | An instruction to produce an unfamiliar experience may presuppose the very capability being taught. |
| Support discovery and correction | Giving the answer can help learning while obscuring what the learner now notices independently. |
| Generalize use | Success with one display, body part, voice or example order may depend on that incidental feature. |

### HCD.6.1:4 - Solution

Design a contrast around what the learner must notice and what that distinction changes in the work. Then use the learner's response to adjust the contrast, support or next task.

#### HCD.6.1:4.1 - Identify the contribution and make it accessible

State the action that needs the distinction and the condition that makes a different action appropriate. Use HCD.3 when the current difficulty could instead arise from inaccessible information, unfamiliar terminology, an execution difficulty or another limiting contribution.

Choose an encounter the learner can enter with available capabilities and support. An existing recording, demonstration, manipulable model or ordinary work episode may suffice. A physical practice needs its own competent design and operating conditions; this pattern supplies no exercise prescription for an unfamiliar or risky movement.

Separate the target experience from the preliminary actions used to make it noticeable. If a demonstration includes preparation, tell the learner what that preparation supplies and when later work would need it. The entire demonstration sequence need not become part of the skill.

#### HCD.6.1:4.2 - Construct a contrast that reveals the distinction

Arrange examples or successive states so that the relevant difference can be encountered. Keep distracting differences limited when they would make the first comparison uninterpretable. For a temporal feature, retain the change and the reference needed to locate it; a picture of the endpoint may lose the target.

Ask for an action that reveals what the learner noticed: point to the changed part, mark an interval, sort the cases, choose a continuation, or demonstrate the difference. A learner need not first possess the expert's vocabulary to make that contribution.

Use the initial response to distinguish plausible difficulties. If the learner notices the contrast but uses another name, connect the name to the already available distinction. If they select by an incidental cue, vary that cue. If the signal is inaccessible, repair access. If the target itself remains unclear, improve the demonstration or explanation.

##### HCD.6.1:4.2.1 - Make a Relation in the Next Explanation Noticeable

When the encounter prepares a later explanation, choose the contrast from the relation that explanation will introduce. The learner needs something they can inspect with their existing actions and then reconnect to the explanation. HCD.6:4.2.2 develops that complete lesson and a worked-solution alternative.

In HCD.6:5.7, keeping two batch times fixed while changing their request counts exposes what a simple average ignores. Scaling both counts together tests a different relation. Asking for one calculation across the cases makes those differences consequential. The learner's attempt shows which relation the subsequent explanation needs to make explicit. If the relation is already accessible, omit that contrast and address the remaining difficulty.

Return the attempt to HCD.6's explanation and fresh application. A learner may notice the difference without yet knowing how to calculate with it; another may calculate correctly after help without having noticed it independently. Preserve that distinction when choosing the next action.


##### HCD.6.1:4.2.2 - Learn a family of regularities without forcing a single rule

Use several examples when a target distinction depends on combinations, timing, context or probabilistic regularities that one pair cannot expose. A natural-language expression may be appropriate in one register and awkward in another; a style may be recognizable through several relations that no isolated feature uniquely identifies. First establish the intended use and the source of qualified examples. A collection chosen for one speaker, teacher or archive can distort the family the learner will later encounter.

Start with examples the learner can meaningfully encounter. Make the context available, including the preceding phrase, action or response when that changes interpretation. Ask for a discriminating contribution: select a likely continuation, match an utterance to a situation, imitate and vary a phrase, respond to a partner, or compare two performances. Supply feedback in a form the learner can use even when a complete verbal rule is unavailable.

Use errors and uncertainty to choose informative comparisons. Put a confusable case beside a clear one; preserve a contextual condition that makes the difference intelligible. Then return to varied examples where the learner must recover that difference among other features. Purely isolated contrasts can make a cue easy to detect while leaving it unavailable in ordinary performance. Conversely, an undirected stream of material can leave the same confusion untouched. Combine broader exposure with focused returns where they make a useful difference.

Choose variation on two grounds: representation of the receiving practice and resolution of a present confusion. Include familiar, uncommon and changing forms according to that purpose. Distinguish an exception to the learner's provisional generalization from a different accepted convention or a defective example. A rare form need not be learned to the same automaticity as an everyday one; a reliable reference or a timely request can be the better contribution.

Do not equate a distribution in teaching material with a rule of the culture. When the material intentionally balances two alternatives, explain that balance if it could mislead expectations about ordinary use. When judgement is graded or contested, preserve more than a forced binary answer: ask which use is more fitting under the stated purpose, what remains uncertain and how a competent participant would respond.

After a response becomes reliable on familiar material, try the relevant change of speaker, phrase, partner or context. Keep the target judgement distinct from the ability to produce the same pattern. Select further encounters when they can improve the needed response or resolve an important uncertainty; exhaustive coverage of the culture is not the completion condition.

#### HCD.6.1:4.3 - Connect the noticed difference to its use


Show what changes because of the distinction. Let the learner make that next move with support appropriate to the present purpose. HCD.9 supplies usable feedback and correction; a score alone does not show what to change.

For human experience, the teacher can arrange conditions and ask what the learner notices. The learner's account may differ from the teacher's wording. Judge the discrimination needed for the work through the relevant response and conditions. The method does not require identical private sensations in two people.

Keep recognition and performance distinguishable. A dancer may recognize that balance was lost while lacking the coordination to prevent it. A learner may correctly locate a sound's release while being unable to reproduce it on an instrument. Those are useful diagnostic results, not reasons to repeat the same explanation indefinitely.

#### HCD.6.1:4.4 - Change incidental features and then combine contributions

Keep the target relation while changing a feature that could have become an unintended cue. Alternatively, change the target while preserving that cue. The learner's response now helps locate what was learned from the first task.

Once the relevant distinctions are accessible, combine those needed together in the encompassing work. HCD.6 prepares sufficiently whole tasks; HCD.10 selects variation and support changes from their purpose. One-at-a-time contrast is a teaching option, not a claim that real work contains only one changing feature.

Choose the next comparison from an actual confusion when one is available. Additional comparisons are useful when they reveal or correct a difference that matters. They need not fill every practice episode.

#### HCD.6.1:4.5 - Decide what the attempt supports and continue

Keep what the learner did, the relevant conditions and any help that supplied the answer recoverable at the grain needed by the next decision. This can be a short note within the existing practice account.

Continue with correction, another contrast, less or different help, or combination in the whole task according to the response. Stop when the present purpose is served. HCD.11–HCD.13 address stronger performance, transfer and retention claims when those claims are needed.

A successful first response supports that response under those conditions. A teacher's chosen contrast remains a design proposal until its use is observed. Neither repetition count nor the presence of all task sections demonstrates the capability.

### HCD.6.1:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.6.1:5.1 - Hearing a release rather than moving the next attack

The learning target in this constructed example is to distinguish sound duration from the interval between attacks. Two recordings have attacks at the same times. In one, the first sound continues until the next attack; in the other, it stops earlier.

The teacher replays the pair and asks the learner to indicate when the first sound ends. A simple timeline may support the first attempt. The next move is to describe or reproduce the intervening silence, with the original attack times retained.

A later pair changes loudness while preserving the timings. Moving the attack merely because the louder sound seems more prominent would expose another cue. A further recording changes the release while keeping loudness fixed. These tasks can separate the relevant temporal distinction from a loudness judgement.

The rhythmic practice supplies the sound, timing and performance criteria. Recognizing the distinction does not itself establish instrument technique.

#### HCD.6.1:5.2 - Distinguishing active work from elapsed time

A trainee sees two requests completed in ten minutes each and treats them as equal demands on an operator's active work. The supplied work records show the operator working continuously on one request, and working for two minutes with eight minutes of waiting on the other.

The trainer asks the learner to mark the operator's active intervals and add their durations: ten minutes for the first request and two for the second. The distinction now changes the calculation of active operator time. It does not determine how long equipment remains occupied or whether the operator is reserved during the wait.

A next case preserves two active minutes but changes the wait. Another preserves the ten-minute completion time while changing active operator time. If the learner still equates elapsed time with active work, the trainer can locate the missed relation. The records must actually show those intervals; completion time alone cannot supply them.

#### HCD.6.1:5.3 - Separating a relation from the way it is drawn

A learner has recognized a shared dependency only when a diagram uses one color for its arrows. The teacher supplies two small constructions with different colors and layouts but the same dependency, and another with the familiar colors but a changed dependency.

The learner identifies which intermediate result both later steps need and explains what would become unavailable if it were removed. The changed drawing can expose reliance on color; the changed relation can expose superficial matching of the whole picture.

This task teaches noticing a relation already supplied by the subject account. Proving a new property of the construction remains another contribution.

#### HCD.6.1:5.4 - Reading what changed in a claim across projects

Two permitted project excerpts describe the same observation. One concludes, "The indicator increased under these measurement conditions." The other concludes, "Increased resistance caused the indicator change." The learner is asked to mark what the second statement adds and what evidence would be needed for that added claim under the supplied subject account. The correct distinction concerns observation and causal attribution; the text's length or confidence of tone is incidental.

The learner then inspects two reports from another project. Both use different wording but derive from the same original observation. Calling them two independent observations would miss a different consequential relation: the provenance is shared. The supplied task criterion determines whether one observation suffices for the receiving use; another report does not create another observation.

A changed pair reverses which excerpt is longer and makes the cautious-sounding version overstate the evidence. Another pair contains genuinely separate observations under the stated independence conditions. The learner must use the grounds rather than choose the cautious tone or reject every strong claim. Feedback addresses the missed relation, followed by an own-case action: preserve, narrow or return the claim for the needed support.

HCD.25 develops how to select and connect such permitted project cases; HCD.24 uses discernible differences in peer judgement. The contrast here prepares recognition. Neither identifying an overclaim nor reading the other project's report establishes competence to conduct its full investigation.

These are teaching designs, not reports of observed learning.

### HCD.6.1:6 - Bias-Annotation

Teachers can mistake what is obvious to them for what is available to the learner. Learners can respond successfully to a supplied cue that will disappear in later work. Preserve those different contributions when interpreting an attempt.

### HCD.6.1:7 - Conformance Checklist

- The target distinction changes a named action or interpretation in the relevant work.
- The learner can enter the encounter with the available preparation and support.
- The contrast makes the target accessible without silently supplying the contribution being judged.
- The response can reveal what was noticed and guide a different next attempt.
- Incidental cues, preparation steps and target actions remain distinguishable.
- A later whole task combines the contributions needed together when that use is required.
- Claims about learning remain limited to the observations and their conditions.

### HCD.6.1:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

**“Just notice it.”** Arrange an encounter that makes the relevant contrast accessible and accept a useful response before requiring expert terminology.

**The example teaches its decoration.** Change color, order, voice, location or another plausible cue while retaining the target relation.

**The preparation becomes a ritual.** Explain what it enabled in the demonstration and whether it is needed in the later starting condition.

**Recognition is counted as execution.** Test the next action separately when it requires additional capability.

### HCD.6.1:9 - Consequences

A previously opaque instruction can become an accessible distinction and a useful next action. The resulting practice also helps separate recognition, vocabulary, access and execution difficulties.

The design requires subject knowledge and attention to the learner's response. It does not supply a universal exercise sequence or ensure that a particular contrast will work for every learner.

### HCD.6.1:10 - Rationale

A term can direct attention only through some usable relation to what the learner encounters. Contrasting cases and states can develop that relation. Varying an incidental feature then asks whether recognition depends on it.

The method sits inside the design of representative practice. It can prepare a constituent contribution before the learner performs the encompassing task, but that larger task determines which distinctions are useful and which combinations must eventually be learned.

### HCD.6.1:11 - SoTA-Echoing

How can a teacher make a needed distinction accessible when repeating the instruction leaves it unnoticed? Adopt the variation-theory choice of arranging variation and invariance around what the learner needs to discern. Kullberg, Ingerman and Marton's [Planning and Analyzing Teaching](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003194903), 2024, develops this answer. It guides §4.2's contrast and §4.4's change of incidental cues; it does not guarantee learning from a prescribed sequence.

Compare this focused work with a supported whole task. The [4C/ID approach](https://www.4cid.org/about/) combines whole learning tasks with supportive information, timely procedural guidance and part practice when needed. If the learner already notices the distinction and needs its name or a procedure, a demonstration within the whole task may suffice. A separate contrast then adds preparation without addressing a missing contribution. When the learner cannot pick out the relevant difference, however, another whole attempt can preserve the same unnoticed cue. The focused contrast makes that relation available for inspection. Its accepted cost is preparing the contrast and interpreting one more response; §4.4 then combines the contribution back into whole-task use.

Adapt comparison selection to the learner's response in §4.4. Jacoby, Massey and Kellman's [2024 study of adaptively triggered comparisons](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39191799/) reports improved learning efficiency in facial-identity experiments when comparisons addressed learners' confusions. Compared with a fixed series, this supplies a reason to spend effort on a confusion that persists and to omit comparisons that no longer change the next task. The empirical result retains its domain and participant limits; it does not validate the rhythmic, service or mathematical examples here.

Subject practice determines correct use, and the representation must retain the relevant distinction. Reconsider the focused contrast if a simpler explanation already enables its use, if the learner selects by another cue, or if inaccessible information or execution is the limiting contribution. These conditions change the contrast, the assistance or the decision to use this method; they do not require completing an exercise series for its own sake.

For a family of perceptual examples, [Uchihara, Karas and Thomson's 2025 meta-analysis](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263125100879) examines high-variability second-language phonetic training combining varied speakers, phonetic contexts and feedback. It supports that training package for perception, with qualified retention and generalization results; it does not isolate every component's causal contribution. Section 4.2.2 adapts the construction question—represent the needed variation and let the learner use informative feedback—while keeping recognition distinct from production. The language application is an illustrative adaptation, not a replication of that protocol.

[Jacoby and colleagues (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01800-9) find shared and culturally differing rhythm priors across the sampled groups. This changes which examples can represent a receiving practice; a laboratory distribution is no aesthetic standard for every community. Reopen the example family when its participants, repertoire or receiving use changes.

### HCD.6.1:12 - Relations

HCD.24 uses a discernible criterion in peer review; HCD.25 arranges comparison and personal return across project cases.

HCD.3 diagnoses the limiting contribution. HCD.5 selects development methods. HCD.6 supplies the whole practice task; this nested method develops its recognition component. HCD.6:4.2.2 and :5.7 connect preparation to a later explanation and compare construction with explaining a worked solution. HCD.9 and HCD.10 guide correction and progression; HCD.11–HCD.13 qualify later claims.

FPF B.5.EA supports a participant who cannot yet express a relevant distinction. B.5.4 supports interpretation through an available concept; B.1.5.EW relates constituent and encompassing work.

NOT.8 can help represent a temporal or embodied distinction; RHY supplies the rhythmic methods used in the first example. Those subject methods remain the source of their own performance criteria.

### HCD.6.1:End

## HCD.7 - Arrange Providers, Access, Tools, and AI Support for Human Capability Development

> **Type:** Human Capability Development practitioner support-arrangement pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### HCD.7:0 - Use This When

Use this pattern when a capability-development programme, Method, or practice set needs contributions from people, sources, tools, AI, an environment, or an organization, and the practitioner must establish what will actually be available. Begin with the concrete functions and their timing: explanation, task preparation, safe access, feedback, checking, independent assessment, specialist input, and fallback. Do not begin with a provider label or a total-hours budget.

The first useful result is an **enabled development arrangement**: each required contribution has an identified supplier, competent and authorized scope, access conditions, capacity at the required time, data and privacy boundary, human checks, fallback, and evidence of availability. If one of these values is missing, return the supported design and the exact unavailable contribution, timing, access condition, or provider result. A plausible design is not an enabled arrangement.

The practical gain is feasibility before participation. The practitioner can see whether feedback arrives before the next attempt, whether peak assessment demand fits the provider window, whether a peer contribution prepares rather than replaces competent assessment, and whether AI support leaves enough human time to check consequential output.

Do not use HCD.7 to create a missing provider capability, infer that a provider is competent from a job title, prove learning from access, or decide that a person is suitable for a class-level arrangement. Use HCD.8 when an exact unavailable contribution needs an obtain-or-build comparison and the preparation or operating test that the chosen route requires. Personal fit remains with the applicable demand, target, profile, programme, and participation decisions.

#### HCD.7:0.1 - Working Terms

| Name in this pattern | What it denotes |
| --- | --- |
| required development contribution | One result or action that the selected programme, Method, or practice needs from a learner, teacher, assessor, specialist, peer, source, tool, AI system, environment, or organization. |
| provider function | The bounded contribution to be supplied, such as explaining, preparing a case, giving actionable feedback, checking a critical error, assessing independently, maintaining access, or supplying a specialist result. A role title does not define the function. |
| provider | The identified person, group, organization, service, or tool relied upon to perform the required action or supply its result under stated conditions. A book or dataset used for that contribution remains an identifiable source with its own edition and access conditions. Different contributions may have different providers. |
| access condition | A permission, credential, data boundary, physical or digital route, timing, environment, interface, or participation condition needed to obtain a contribution. |
| capacity window | The amount and timing of provider attention or system availability that can serve the required work, including concurrency and peak demand. A total can fit while a critical window fails. |
| human-check contribution | The human judgement, verification, explanation, authorization, or accountability that remains necessary when AI or another tool assists. It has its own competence and workload. |
| fallback | A separately feasible way to preserve the required result or return safely when the preferred provider, tool, data, or timing becomes unavailable. |
| enabled development arrangement | The contribution allocation plus established providers, access, capacity, constraints, checks, fallback, and evidence sufficient to begin the bounded development use. It does not establish that the use occurred or succeeded. |

Intended help in a programme, help permitted by a practice task, help actually available, and help received in an attempt are different facts. HCD.7 establishes actual availability; HCD.9 and HCD.11 preserve what was received and what the resulting attempt can support.

### HCD.7:1 - Problem Frame

A programme can describe excellent practice and still be impossible to run. The teacher may have enough annual hours but not enough time during final assessments. The relevant project data may be inaccessible. A specialist may be available only after the decision deadline. An AI tool may be permitted for public material but prohibited for the learner's project. A peer group may generate useful questions while lacking the competence or independence required for assessment.

Support is not one undifferentiated resource. Explanation, coaching, task preparation, feedback, technical access, domain checking, independent assessment, and specialist judgement have different competence, timing, privacy, and authority conditions. Replacing one with another can change both the learning activity and the evidence it yields.

The practitioner therefore has to allocate exact contributions, test actual availability and peak capacity, and preserve human checking and fallback rather than treating provider names, aggregate hours, or tool access as proof of an operating arrangement.

### HCD.7:2 - Problem

The common shortcut is provider-by-label: a teacher, mentor, community, apprenticeship, platform, or AI tutor is assumed to supply every support function. The label hides task competence, assessment independence, access, supervision, workload, and the conditions under which the contribution is legitimate.

A second shortcut divides a total by the number of learners. The resulting “hours per learner” can be useful for costing but says nothing about individual contact, concurrency, feedback latency, or a final-week peak. Shared meetings also do not supply additional individual checking merely because more people attend.

A third shortcut treats automated assistance as free capacity. Searching, drafting, or calculating can reduce one burden and create another: prompt preparation, source checking, error challenge, data protection, and fallback. The arrangement needs a contribution account that remains true under actual use.

### HCD.7:3 - Forces

- Aggregate capacity is easy to budget, while timing, concurrency, feedback deadlines, and peak load determine actual service.
- A provider title is easy to name, while competence and authority are contribution-specific.
- Peer participation can broaden feedback and reflection, while independent or high-consequence judgement may require another qualified assessor.
- AI can accelerate search, generation, calculation, or critique, while human checking and data governance consume real capacity.
- Supported performance can improve the immediate result, while it does not establish unaided capability or retained performance after support changes.
- One platform or community can host many functions, while access, facilitation, leadership, task expertise, and coordination remain distinct contributions.
- A standard arrangement supports class planning, while personal needs and participation conditions become known only for an identified learner.
- Redundancy improves resilience, while a nominal fallback that lacks competence, access, or time is not feasible.
- HCD can expose the required support, while employment, privacy, safety, legal, clinical, target-domain, and organizational owners retain their decisions.

### HCD.7:4 - Solution

Translate the selected programme, Method, and practice tasks into required contributions; assign each contribution to an identified provider or resource; and test competence, access, timing, capacity, constraints, human checking, and fallback before calling the arrangement enabled.

#### HCD.7:4.1 - Bind the Development Use

Name:

1. the human holder or defined learner class, participation basis, programme or practice recipient, and receiving decision;
2. the later-Work target, selected HCD.5 Method, HCD.6 practice set, required work products, protected errors, and intended evidence uses;
3. the calendar, attempt and feedback timing, learner workload, provider windows, peak periods, and decision deadlines;
4. project, source, data, environment, tool, AI, privacy, confidentiality, accessibility, permission, safety, and authority conditions; and
5. every direct owner whose competence, result, or authorization the arrangement consumes.

For a class-level design, state the audience assumptions and capacity range. Do not infer that a particular person fits the arrangement. When that person becomes known, recheck their task, access, participation, support, and accommodation conditions rather than inheriting the class average.

#### HCD.7:4.2 - Allocate Contributions, Not Labels

Construct one contribution allocation:

| Allocation field | Required content |
| --- | --- |
| contribution and recipient | The explanation, demonstration, case, access, feedback, check, assessment, specialist result, coordination, or fallback needed; who or what uses it; and which task or result it enables. |
| provider and scope | Identified supplier, contribution-specific competence, authorization, independence where needed, and explicit non-responsibilities. |
| timing and service condition | Required date or interval, concurrency, response or feedback deadline, duration, handoff, and dependency on other contributions. |
| access and constraints | Data, source, project, environment, interface, accessibility, privacy, confidentiality, safety, legal, employment, or organizational conditions. |
| capacity | Preparation, delivery, checking, correction, coordination, fallback, and peak-load effort; competing uses and unavailable periods. |
| evidence and fallback | Evidence that the provider and access are available for this use; failure signal; feasible fallback or exact missing result and retry condition. |

One person or tool may supply several contributions, but each keeps its own competence, workload, and constraints. Several providers may jointly supply one result, but their interfaces and the person responsible for the final judgement remain explicit. A catalogue, contract, platform account, or calendar slot is evidence input; none establishes every contribution by itself.

#### HCD.7:4.3 - Test Competence, Access, Timing, and Capacity

For each contribution:

1. **Check competence and scope.** Obtain evidence suitable for the task and consequence. Familiarity with content, teaching ability, domain judgement, facilitation, and independent assessment are not interchangeable.
2. **Check authority and independence.** State who may provide feedback, access confidential data, change a project, judge a protected criterion, authorize a retry, or make the later decision. A helpful participant is not automatically the authorized assessor.
3. **Check actual access.** Verify source edition or data, credentials, project permission, environment, tool or model availability, interface, and accessibility during the required window.
4. **Check total and peak capacity.** Include preparation, learner contact, review, correction, coordination, disputes, fallback, and competing work. Test the busiest window and the promised feedback interval, not only the total.
5. **Check handoffs and fallback.** Make the next provider, due time, result form, and failure signal visible. A fallback is feasible only when its competence, access, capacity, and authority also fit.
6. **Return exact gaps.** If a contribution is unavailable, state the blocked practice or evidence use, current supported design, safe interim boundary, and retry condition. Use HCD.8 when obtaining or building that contribution must be compared; a build decision is not a prerequisite to that comparison.

An enabled arrangement can be small: one learner, one task, a source, a teacher feedback window, an assessor, and a fallback. It need not establish a complete institutional service when the bounded use needs less.

#### HCD.7:4.4 - Arrange AI and Tool Support without Attribution Drift

For each AI or tool use, state:

- the exact permitted contribution, such as search, example generation, calculation, drafting, critique, translation, or accessibility support;
- the data and confidentiality boundary, model or tool condition when it changes risk, and prohibited uses;
- the human action that remains, including selection, source verification, assumption and calculation checks, error challenge, explanation, judgement, or authorization;
- time for prompting, checking, correction, escalation, and recording support actually received;
- a fallback for outage, unsafe output, incompatible data, or unacceptable uncertainty; and
- which practice or evidence uses require a changed-support or unassisted attempt.

AI access can improve equipped performance without establishing human learning. A no-AI observation answers only the bounded contribution and conditions it was designed to expose. HCD.10 selects a justified support change; HCD.11–HCD.13 interpret the resulting evidence.

#### HCD.7:4.5 - Keep Peer, Teacher, Assessor, and Specialist Work Distinct

Peers can expose alternative reasoning, rehearse feedback, notice a question, and help a learner prepare a revision. Those contributions can reduce avoidable teacher burden. They do not replace a teacher or assessor contribution whose result needs task competence, calibration, independence, authority, or a protected-error judgement.

A teacher may explain and coach while another assessor judges the independent result. A specialist may supply a bounded domain fact without teaching the whole task. An organization may enable project access without becoming the capability holder. State each contribution and handoff rather than turning all participants into one generic support role.

#### HCD.7:4.6 - Return the Arrangement or Exact Missing Contribution

An HCD.7 result contains:

| Result position | Required content |
| --- | --- |
| arrangement boundary | Human holder or learner class, programme or practice, later-Work target, participation, calendar, evidence uses, protected conditions, and receiving decision. |
| contribution allocation | Every required learner, reference, tool, AI, peer, teacher, assessor, specialist, environment, organization, and fallback contribution. |
| provider basis | Supplier, competence, scope, authority, independence, access, data boundary, timing, capacity, peak load, and evidence of availability for each contribution. |
| human checking and attribution | Consequential AI or tool outputs, required human checks, checking capacity, and the distinction among joint, supported, and independent performance. |
| coordination and fallback | Handoffs, deadlines, failure signals, dispute path, and feasible fallback conditions. |
| disposition | `enabled development arrangement`, `supported design with exact missing contribution`, or `class arrangement awaiting personal fit`. |
| continuation | Practice start condition, personal-fit input, HCD.8 obtain-or-build question, provider return, schedule or capacity change, or smallest condition that reopens the arrangement. |

Call the arrangement enabled only when every contribution needed for the bounded start and evidence use has a supported provider, access route, capacity window, and fallback or safe stop. A missing later optional contribution need not block an earlier independent result; state its reach rather than declaring the whole design impossible.

#### HCD.7:4.7 - Recognition and Assurance

**Recognition.** Use HCD.7 when a plan says “a teacher will support,” “peers will review,” “the platform provides feedback,” or “AI will help,” but the concrete contribution, recipient, timing, capacity, human check, or fallback is still unclear.

**Assurance.** Stronger reliance needs contribution-specific competence and authority, actual access during the required window, total and peak capacity, privacy and safety conditions, feasible handoffs and fallback, and evidence appropriate to the protected result. Service operation, provider competence, learning, transfer, and retention remain separate conclusions.

#### HCD.7:4.8 - What Changes in Practice

A practitioner stops asking, “Do we have a teacher and an AI tool?” and asks, “Which exact contribution must reach which learner or task, who can supply it under these data and authority conditions, does capacity fit the critical window, what human checking remains, and what happens when it fails?” Missing support becomes a named result, not a surprise during practice.

### HCD.7:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### HCD.7:5.1 - Twelve Participants and the 240-Hour Teacher Account

The FoundationsProgramme class design has twelve participants, thirty-two ordinary weeks, and two final weeks. An ordinary week allocates 1.5 teacher hours to group review, 3 hours to checking twelve short results, 1 hour to case and source preparation, and 1 hour to individual difficulties and assessment calibration: 6.5 hours. Each final week requires 16 hours, including individual reading, conversations, subgroup review, calibration, repeat checks, and a small delay or disagreement reserve.

The total is `32 × 6.5 + 2 × 16 = 240` teacher hours. Dividing by twelve gives a costing allocation of 20 hours per participant; it does not promise twenty individual-contact hours. The arrangement is enabled only if the two sixteen-hour peaks are reserved and ordinary feedback can arrive before the next two-week block.

With twenty-four participants, the original checking and conversation rows no longer fit. A single larger group meeting supplies no additional individual review. The supported return is to double the relevant checking capacity, divide the group with competent providers, reduce or redesign the promised contribution, or delay launch. HCD.7 does not call the larger class enabled merely because 240 total hours still appear in a budget.

#### HCD.7:5.2 - Supply Both Sides of Peer Learning and the Required Assessment

Participants learn to judge whether a diagnostic recommendation follows from its evidence and to revise their own work. A peer compares two permitted observation-to-conclusion fragments, identifies the relevant condition and writes a grounded comment. The author explains why to use or reject the comment, then makes the warranted revision. HCD.24 develops this bilateral exchange. The reviewer's judgement and the author's response are learning contributions even when no teacher time is saved.

Allocate accessible cases, criterion preparation, the peer's reading and judgement, the author's response and correction, and a qualified dispute window before the next block. If peers agree on an unsupported cause, a prepared teacher resolves the narrow subject question and returns its ground to both sides; each then performs the affected action again. Record the supplied help. A learner's comment does not become an independent protected-error judgement merely because it is useful.

The teacher or designated assessor still applies the target-domain criteria to the consequential assessment result. Peer preparation can reduce search and coordination burden, while the amount saved remains to be observed. Keeping the learning purpose and the required assessor contribution distinct prevents one from silently replacing the other.

For a final attempt, the arrangement separately allocates reading, an individual conversation, possible correction, and a calibrated repeat check. If the named teacher is unavailable, a prepared colleague with compatible competence and access can be the fallback; otherwise the final week moves. A calendar placeholder or unprepared substitute is not a fallback.

#### HCD.7:5.3 - AI Search and Critique with Human Checking

AI may search public sources, propose examples, calculate, draft, or critique within the permitted data boundary. The learner first states the question and acceptable-result condition, then checks decisive sources, assumptions, configuration, and calculations and explains why the selected Method applies. A human assessor retains the final protected-error judgement.

The capacity account includes preparation of permitted prompts, checking consequential output, correcting failures, and a path for closed project data that cannot be sent to the tool. A narrow changed-support task can make one human contribution visible, but ordinary AI-supported work remains legitimate when the later-Work configuration includes it. Neither access nor fluent output establishes learning.

#### HCD.7:5.4 - Project Access Missing before Practice

A learner and teacher are available, but the planned workplace task requires project data and permission for a small safe trial that the organization has not granted. The arrangement returns the exact data, authorization, owner, affected task, and retry condition. A stipulated teaching case can preserve an earlier practice use, but it cannot be reported as the workplace result. HCD.8 can compare obtaining an alternative contribution with building an environment or provider capability when that exact gap must be closed for the selected practice.

#### HCD.7:5.5 - Prepare Mentor Help before Counting It as Capacity

Two prospective mentors will help groups compare rival diagnostic explanations. Give each a qualified case, the intended personal action, representative learner mistakes and the limits of the mentor's authority. Each independently selects a response to the same two learner attempts, explains its grounds and identifies the question that would require a specialist. A prepared teacher compares their responses against the case criteria, corrects incompatible advice and observes another attempt where needed. HCD.8 supplies the obtain-or-build and operating-test work if that competence is still missing.

For the pump case, an AI suggestion asks the learner to take a fresh pressure reading. The mentor must notice that this variant already supplies the reading and allows no further worthwhile observation. They reject that suggestion, use the qualified reference to ask about the pressure implication, and leave the model-selection operation with the learner. If the subject implication itself is unresolved, the mentor returns that exact question rather than improvising a criterion.

This is an application of §4.4's existing human-check arrangement. Access to the suggestion tool adds no qualified mentor until the person can select, adapt or reject its output in the actual task. Reserve preparation, checking, live help and fallback separately. For example, two thirty-minute mentor preparation attempts and forty minutes of teacher comparison allocate 100 provider-minutes before live delivery. Include those minutes once in the product's fixed preparation; count live windows and subsequent maintenance where they actually fall.

[Tutor CoPilot, November 2025 revision](https://edworkingpapers.com/sites/default/files/ai24_1054_v2.pdf) supplies a bounded example of tutor-facing suggestions built from expert reasoning with human selection and editing. Its paid professional tutors received training; the study does not establish that unprepared volunteers can replace them, nor that exit-ticket effects show distant transfer or independent tutor learning. Its tool price is not a complete support cost. The diagnostic preparation above is an authored application, not that study's observed result.

#### HCD.7:5.6 - One Learner Can Start with Available Feedback

In this fictional case, a learner has agreed to practise making a catalogue record from a supplied photograph and its metadata. The selected task uses anonymized dataset D2 and rubric R3; one protected error is inventing a date when the supplied information requires an "unknown" entry. The learner may use the rubric and write the practice record on paper or in the practice folder. The teacher is authorized to give formative feedback and check this error, and has already judged two representative records correctly against R3 within the required checking time.

The learner has reserved 09:00–09:40. The teacher has confirmed eight minutes before 09:00 to prepare the task, verify D2/R3 compatibility and access, and confirm the appointments; five minutes at 09:10–09:15 for feedback on the first record; seven minutes at 09:25–09:32 to check the correction; and five minutes at 09:32–09:37 for a question, further correction or rescheduling. The full teacher allocation is `8 + 5 + 7 + 5 = 25` minutes, with no competing work in those slots. The learner makes the first record at 09:00–09:10, receives feedback, then revises it at 09:15–09:25; the checking and reserve also fit the learner's window.

Both can open the specified materials, and permitted printed copies have been checked for the same content. Those copies preserve access if the folder fails. If the teacher misses the feedback slot, the learner saves the first record and reschedules feedback and correction; access to R3 alone does not complete that cycle.

The result is an **enabled development arrangement for this one supported attempt and correction**. D2 and R3 remain the data and criteria being used; the teacher supplies feedback and checking. No additional provider preparation is currently needed. The practice has not yet occurred, and later independent assessment would need its own arrangement.

### HCD.7:6 - Bias-Annotation

Lenses: **Gov**, **Arch**, **Onto/Epist**, **Prag**, **Did**. Scope: arranging actually available provider, access, tool, AI, environment, and human-check contributions for bounded capability-development use.

| Recurring bias | Likely drift | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| provider-label bias | “Teacher,” “mentor,” “community,” or “platform” is assumed to supply all functions. | Allocate contribution-specific competence, authority, timing, capacity, and constraints. |
| aggregate-hours bias | A total or per-person quotient is treated as service availability. | Test feedback deadlines, concurrency, individual work, and peak periods. |
| automation-free-capacity bias | AI assistance is counted without prompting, checking, correction, escalation, or fallback. | Put the human-check contribution and its workload in the allocation. |
| peer-substitution bias | Peer participation replaces independent or competent assessment. | State the peer's learning and support contributions and retain the required assessor result. |
| access-by-account bias | A login, licence, or repository membership is treated as usable access. | Verify data, permissions, interface, timing, accessibility, and task compatibility. |
| class-average bias | A class arrangement is assumed suitable for every participant. | Recheck personal task, participation, access, support, and accommodation conditions. |
| nominal-fallback bias | An unprepared substitute or delayed source is called resilient capacity. | Test the fallback against the same competence, access, timing, and authority positions. |
| supported-capability bias | Equipped output or supervised participation becomes a human capability claim. | Preserve support conditions and route stronger evidence to HCD.11–HCD.13. |

### HCD.7:7 - Conformance Checklist

- [ ] The human holder or learner class, participation basis, programme or practice, later-Work target, calendar, evidence uses, and receiving decision are explicit.
- [ ] Every required explanation, preparation, access, feedback, checking, assessment, specialist, coordination, environment, and fallback contribution is identifiable with its recipient and conditions.
- [ ] Provider competence, scope, authority, and independence are supported for the exact contribution rather than inferred from a role label.
- [ ] Data, source, project, tool, AI, interface, privacy, confidentiality, accessibility, safety, legal, and organizational conditions are explicit where material.
- [ ] Total capacity includes preparation, delivery, review, correction, coordination, disagreement, fallback, and competing work.
- [ ] Peak periods, concurrency, feedback deadlines, and handoff times fit the actual provider windows.
- [ ] Peer, teacher, assessor, specialist, organization, source, tool, and AI contributions remain distinct.
- [ ] AI and tool contributions state permitted work, prohibited data or use, human checks, checking capacity, attribution, and fallback.
- [ ] Intended help, permitted help, actual availability, received help, joint performance, and independent performance are not conflated.
- [ ] A fallback satisfies the same relevant competence, access, capacity, timing, and authority conditions or is reported as unavailable.
- [ ] A class-level arrangement retains personal-fit and participation questions for the named learner.
- [ ] The disposition says which bounded use can start and returns each exact missing contribution without claiming provider creation, service operation, learning, transfer, or retention.

### HCD.7:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “We have 20 teacher hours per learner” | A costing allocation is mistaken for individual contact and peak capacity. | Reconstruct the actual shared, individual, preparation, checking, and final-week rows. |
| “One meeting supports twice the class” | Individual checking and conversations grow even when group time does not. | Add competent capacity, divide the group, redesign the contribution, or delay. |
| “Peers can grade it” | Peer review may lack domain competence, calibration, independence, or authority. | Use peers to prepare feedback and preserve the qualified assessor contribution. |
| “The platform gives feedback” | The provider, information content, latency, and correction opportunity are hidden. | Name the exact feedback contribution and its evidence, timing, and recipient. |
| “AI saves the teacher's time” | Prompting, checking, correction, data limits, and escalations are omitted. | Compare the complete human-plus-tool workload and preserve consequential judgement. |
| “A licence means access” | Credentials can coexist with missing data, permission, interface, or usable timing. | Test access for the actual task and window. |
| “Supervised participation proves capability” | Participation, entrusted access, and supported output answer different questions. | Record the support configuration and obtain the applicable performance evidence. |
| “We should train every provider” | Existing qualified contributions are ignored and HCD.8 becomes ritual. | Use the available provider; build only the exact missing capability. |

### HCD.7:9 - Consequences

The practitioner gains a launch boundary grounded in real contributions rather than names or totals. Capacity bottlenecks, data restrictions, assessment independence, AI checking, and fallback become visible early enough to redesign the arrangement or return a precise missing result.

The cost is service-level detail. Provider competence, access, schedules, peak loads, handoffs, and privacy conditions must be checked, and some attractive programme designs will remain disabled. A class design may still need personal adaptation, and an enabled arrangement still supplies no evidence that learning occurred.

### HCD.7:10 - Rationale

Development support is a configuration of contributions. Its feasibility depends on the relation among task, provider, recipient, timing, access, capacity, and consequence. Provider names and aggregate resources erase those relations and make substitution look easier than it is.

Separating intended, permitted, available, and received help protects both design and evidence. Explicit human checking prevents automation from hiding labour or reallocating consequential judgement without notice. A precise missing-contribution return gives HCD.8 or another owner a real obtain-or-build question instead of a generic demand for more support.

### HCD.7:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The working question is: **How should a practitioner establish that the people, access, tools, AI, and other support needed by a development use are actually available at the required competence, time, capacity, and consequence boundary?**

The selected best-known line treats support as a configuration of distinct provider, access, coordination, and checking contributions rather than as a provider label. Brooks and colleagues' 2024 qualitative study of learning-health-system communities ([`SOC-05`](https://doi.org/10.1002/lrh2.10412)) makes people, platform, facilitation, leadership, and resource contributions separately visible; it supplies arrangement questions, not a causal capability effect. Matsuo and Tsukube's 2020 cognitive-apprenticeship review ([`SOC-02`](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijme.2020.100417)) supports distinguishing modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration while leaving their sequence and workplace transfer conditional. HCD.7 adapts those contributions into the allocation and service tests in §§4.2–4.5.

The serious ordinary alternative is label-and-total planning: name a teacher, mentor, community, apprenticeship, or platform, total the available hours, and assume the functions will be supplied. It is cheaper to plan, but it hides competence, individual work, peak load, access, privacy, assessment independence, and fallback. HCD.7 rejects the provider label and aggregate total as sufficiency evidence while retaining them as inputs to a complete contribution account.

Tullis, Goldstone, and Hanson's 2015 experiment ([`COG-11`](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222895.2015.1008686)) is direct limit evidence that assistance improving practice can impair later unassisted performance and that support scheduling matters in its laboratory motor task; it does not prescribe a universal fading schedule or occupational arrangement. Wiese, Kilty, and Bennett's 2018 clinical realist synthesis ([`SOC-03`](https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13655)) shows that supervised participation and graduated access depend on task risk, trust, learner position, and service pressure; its clinical governance does not transfer wholesale. Dell’Acqua and colleagues' bounded field experiment ([`AI-03`](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.21838)) supports independent error challenge under specific task and model conditions, not a stable universal AI frontier. These limits produce the support-state, human-check, and changed-support boundaries in §§4.3–4.7.
