- [FPF A.3.1.FT](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/FPF-Spec.md#a31ft---qualify-method-fit-and-transfer) supplies method fit and transfer; **HCD** supplies the learning needed for a later performance.
- **CB.8** addresses conduct that prevents the exchange; **CB.10** helps judge the relationship's value and **CB.11** helps decide its continuation.

### CB.15:End

## CB.16 - Form and Carry a Collective Voice into a Decision

> **Type:** Community-building method pattern
> **Status:** Stable

### CB.16:1 - Problem frame

Use this pattern when a community needs to contribute to a decision that affects its practice, but individual comments do not adequately carry the shared concern. A profession is invited only after consequential design choices have been made. A provider asks a network for its view on a proposed change. Several local groups want to make one request while preserving different interests.

The governed object is a collective contribution to a specified receiving decision: the position, whom it represents, the authority to carry it, and the returned response. This is one branch of collective action. CB.13 constructs the decision mandate when needed; this pattern develops and carries the substantive position within it.

**First useful result:** participants can identify the receiving decision, the useful contribution they seek, the positions and uncertainties that matter, and who may present which position on whose behalf.

**What changes in practice:** a spokesperson can offer a grounded, authorised contribution and bring back an actionable answer. Members can distinguish what they asked for, what was agreed and what remains unresolved.

An individual's sufficiently useful expert answer can remain an individual contribution through CB.5. A community's internal allocation belongs to its existing decision arrangement. Use this pattern when representation of a shared position and its return from another decision are material to the result.

### CB.16:2 - Problem

An organiser may speak confidently for a community without knowing whether its members support the position. A popular statement may omit the practitioners most affected. Conversely, waiting for complete agreement can prevent any useful contribution before the decision closes.

Even a properly authorised message can fail because it asks only for recognition, gives the recipient no feasible action or reaches someone who cannot decide. A meeting may then be reported as influence although the receiving decision and working conditions remain unchanged.

The task is to build a contribution that both the represented participants and the decision-maker can use, carry it under a valid mandate, and return its actual effect and remaining work.

### CB.16:3 - Forces

| Force | Tension |
| --- | --- |
| Shared voice | A joint position can make a common concern intelligible while concealing real differences. |
| Expertise and authority | Knowledge supports the content; representation depends on the group's decision arrangement. |
| Timing | A decision window can be short while affected people need a usable opportunity to contribute. |
| Feasibility | An ambitious request may matter but require contributions that the community cannot provide or promise. |
| Negotiation | A representative needs enough discretion to respond while preserving the limits members accepted. |
| Influence | A received or accepted proposal still needs effective decisions and later observation of the practical result. |

### CB.16:4 - Solution

Locate the decision that can change the practice, develop the useful contribution with the people concerned, obtain the mandate to carry it and engage the actual recipient. Return the response and its consequences to the represented participants before treating the contribution as complete.

#### CB.16:4.1 - Locate the receiving decision and the practical gain

Recover the proposed change or recurring exclusion from an actual source: a decision proposal, current arrangement, invitation or account of the work. Identify who can decide, what is still open, the constraints and the time by which a contribution can matter. Confirm uncertainty with the recipient when access permits.

Ask practitioners what difference they need. Describe the receiving task or result and how the current arrangement helps or defeats it. “Include the technical writer before the interface is fixed so that operating instructions can influence its design” gives a recipient more to assess than “recognise the importance of writers”.

Use STR.5 when the contribution itself is unclear. It connects a recipient's need with a worthwhile result and the capability and resources that could sustain provision. Compare a serious alternative, such as an earlier bounded review, a later specialist service or a different provider. Keep the conditions each proposal needs.

Separate the community's aspiration from the facts on which it relies. Cases may demonstrate a recurring missing input without proving the effect of a proposed new arrangement. Obtain a sufficient source answer or the needed inquiry through CB.14/RMP where that stronger claim determines the choice.

If the decision is already closed, establish what can still change: implementation, correction, a later review or a new decision. Do not offer participants a choice that the recipient has no authority or opportunity to make.

#### CB.16:4.2 - Recover positions and affected differences

Define whose position is needed for this contribution. Use actual membership and constituency arrangements where they exist. Include people affected by the proposed action even when they do not attend ordinary meetings. CB.1 and OCE.2 help recover missing participants and different interests.

Provide enough of the proposal and its consequences for people to respond. Ask for the change they want, the case or reason behind it, what they can accept and what would make the proposal unworkable. Choose accessible routes and timing proportionate to the decision; one open meeting may not reach dispersed or less confident contributors.

Separate agreement, disagreement and absence of a response. An unanswered invitation supplies no assent. A well-attended discussion supplies useful positions, but its participants do not automatically represent every practitioner in the field.

Investigate differences that could change the request. Some may concern the same aim under different conditions; others involve competing priorities or a cost one group is asked to bear. Preserve the consequential difference in the proposal or in a clearly attributed dissent.

Agree what may be quoted, summarised or disclosed. A confidential case can inform the question without being identifiable in the public position. Obtain permitted evidence sufficient for the claim, or narrow it to what the participants can support.

#### CB.16:4.3 - Develop a position the recipient can act on

Construct the contribution around the actual decision. Explain the current difficulty, the proposed change, why it helps the receiving work, the evidence and limits, and the support needed to make it feasible. State what response is requested: a decision, a change to a proposal, a trial, information or a further conversation.

Compare materially different options when the choice remains open. Include the useful part of the current arrangement and the loss each change introduces. A narrower feasible request may obtain a needed contribution sooner; a broader request may be necessary if the narrow one leaves the real problem intact. Explain the choice to the represented participants.

Make the resource implications visible. State what the community can offer within its actual commitments and what must come from the recipient or another owner. A group of practitioners can propose protected review time; it cannot create that allocation by promising enthusiasm.

Prepare a joint position that can carry meaningful disagreement. Depending on the group's rules, it may be a supported majority proposal with a minority account, a common minimum with stated unresolved questions, or several attributed alternatives. Use a joint position only at the scope the participants have authorised.

If the contribution is advice, say what it can establish and which decision remains with its receiver. A request to be consulted may be justified by a useful professional contribution; it does not by itself establish an exclusive right to represent the domain.

#### CB.16:4.4 - Obtain and bound the representation mandate

Use the existing decision arrangement or obtain the needed one through CB.13. Establish who may approve the position, which participants it represents, the authorised spokesperson, the subject and duration, and how members can correct or withdraw the mandate.

Give the representative workable discretion. State what they may clarify or negotiate, the conditions they must preserve and which changes must return for a further decision. A mandate that only says “speak for us” leaves both the speaker and members exposed to incompatible expectations.

Distinguish approval of the position from approval of commitments. The community may authorise a request while each employer, site or individual retains the right to provide its own time or resources. Obtain those decisions when the negotiated action depends on them.

Prepare the spokesperson to use the mandate. They need the reasons, evidence limits, different positions, likely questions and a way to return an unexpected proposal. LDR.1 supplies the working brief and explanation. Where the task needs more than one kind of knowledge, obtain a supporting contributor.

When a collective mandate cannot be obtained within the decision window, choose a truthful narrower contribution. Named willing contributors may offer their own joint view under their own authority. State whom it represents; a community name or large mailing list does not enlarge that scope.

#### CB.16:4.5 - Engage the recipient and handle a changed proposal

Confirm that the recipient can receive the contribution in time and through a usable route. Present the request with its practical reason, represented constituency and mandate. Provide the evidence needed for the decision at a level the recipient can inspect.

If the first contact cannot decide, ask for the appropriate receiving route. Where no accessible route or timely decision remains, return that limit to the participants so they can choose a later opportunity or end this episode.

Use the exchange to test understanding. Ask the recipient to identify the question they can decide and any missing condition. Recover objections from the work: an unavailable resource, another affected interest, an unsupported claim or a different decision boundary may each require a different response.

Work within the authorised discretion. A representative can clarify the case or compare an allowed option. A materially different commitment or claim returns to the people who can approve it. State the pending condition to the recipient so that a provisional discussion is not mistaken for an agreement.

Keep disagreement intelligible. The recipient may decline the request for a reason members contest. Return that reason and the remaining possible action; do not replace it with an unsupported account of the recipient's motives.

If the recipient offers a trial or accepts a change, identify the actual decision, owner, scope and next contribution. Obtain the assignments, access and resources through their owners. An invitation to discuss, a favourable comment and an effective decision remain different results.

#### CB.16:4.6 - Return the answer and make the next action usable

Report the contribution and response to the represented participants. Explain what the recipient accepted, rejected, changed or left open; the reason and evidence supplied; any commitment made within the mandate; and any new question requiring the group's decision.

Give dissenting or previously absent participants a usable opportunity to correct a misrepresentation. Correct a materially inaccurate account with the recipient as well as within the community. CB.13 supplies reconsideration or replacement when the representative exceeded the mandate.

Return implementation work to its actual owners. Use OCE.14 for a bounded revision of an existing arrangement and OCE.6 for needed assignments and enabling conditions. CB.14 supplies a new practice contribution; HCD supplies a needed learning result. If the community has only obtained an invitation to further work, preserve that bounded gain and the unfinished result.

Agree an observation that can tell whether the expected practical change occurred. For example, check whether writers were actually included before the specified decision and whether their contribution was usable. CB.10 can connect those observations with the community's value question. A causal claim about the whole intervention still requires suitable evidence.

Close the representation episode when the answer, effective commitments and remaining work are understood by their recipients. A refusal or a bounded agreement may complete this episode even though the community's wider aim remains open.

#### CB.16:4.7 - Reconsider the position and its continuing mandate

Reopen the affected position when the external proposal changes, new evidence defeats a reason, a previously missed constituency matters, the required provision is absent or the mandate expires. Recover which part of the earlier contribution remains useful.

For continuing representation, agree how the community will keep the representative informed, obtain returns and replace them. The burden may justify a standing arrangement through CB.13; occasional external requests may need only bounded assignments.

Preserve independence among the represented groups. They may support one shared request while retaining different practices and other positions. A cross-community response through CB.15 needs each side's actual mandate at the scope attributed to it.

Independent carriers of a practice can use a published argument or contribute an attributed response without joining a common organisation. Their use or silence supplies no authority for a spokesperson to claim that they endorse the collective position.

### CB.16:5 - Archetypal Grounding

#### CB.16:5.1 - Technical writers ask to enter a design decision earlier

In a constructed engineering firm, a writers' community finds three cases where documentation began after the operating interface had been fixed. The writers had to describe confusing actions that an earlier review might have changed. They recover the cases with the relevant project staff and obtain permission to use the examples internally.

The community compares two proposals. A stronger final documentation service preserves the current development schedule but leaves interface changes late. A bounded writer review before the interface decision could expose explanation problems earlier; it requires time from both a writer and the design team.

Members support trying the early review on two projects. Some prefer a permanent writer on every team, while others cannot provide additional time under current allocations. The position retains those differences and requests a limited trial with protected time, a defined review question and a return after the two project decisions.

Under its member decision arrangement, the community authorises a spokesperson to request that trial. The mandate permits clarification of timing and review material; it does not permit promising staff from every department. The spokesperson brings the two alternatives and the cases to the engineering manager who owns the relevant process decision.

The manager proposes involving all writers in a weekly meeting. That exceeds the offered contribution and lacks time provision. The spokesperson returns the proposal for discussion. The members retain the bounded review, and the manager instead approves two project-specific sessions. The participating managers allocate the agreed time and the two writers accept the work.

The community receives the decision, conditions and named project returns. In the first session, the writer's explanation of an operating sequence prompts the team to clarify an interface label before its decision. Before the second session, its assigned writer becomes unavailable. The project reaches the interface decision before a replacement is obtained and reports that the early review did not occur. The community returns that provision failure to the participating manager for the next proposed use, retaining the useful first contribution. The two returns do not establish the programme's overall effect.

#### CB.16:5.2 - A shared response can preserve a minority concern

A provider proposes moving a network's support sessions to a new time. Most participating groups prefer the new slot; a smaller group would lose its only accessible session. The network gathers each group's reason and confirms which service decisions the provider can make.

Its authorised position supports the new slot only if a usable alternative remains for the affected group. The spokesperson is permitted to compare equivalent alternatives but must return any proposal that removes access. The provider offers a recorded presentation.

The smaller group explains that it needs live questions about its cases, so a recording does not supply the missing contribution. The spokesperson returns that answer within the mandate. The provider agrees to test a second live session if an appropriate host can be assigned. The network reports the conditional result and the unfilled host requirement; access is not described as secured until that condition is met.

#### CB.16:5.3 - Named contributors speak without claiming the whole field

A platform invites comments from repair practitioners on a proposed information form. Several members of a loose network have useful experience, but the network has no authorised common position and many independent repairers are outside it.

The willing contributors submit a joint technical account in their own names, stating the settings their examples cover and the limits of their agreement. They make the permitted account available for others to use or challenge. The response is a real contribution; it is not presented as the view of all repairers.

A later proposal to maintain an ongoing representative relationship would require a mandate and provision through CB.13. The earlier signatures do not settle that new question.

#### CB.16:5.4 - A request already within the organiser's assignment

A club needs its existing room booking corrected. The authorised organiser contacts the venue, obtains the correction and informs participants. The task is complete under the existing assignment. It does not need a new collective position or representation process.

### CB.16:6 - Bias-Annotation

A spokesperson may overrepresent confident contributors, people available at the consultation time or the position most convenient to a sponsor. Invitations from a prestigious recipient can also encourage overclaiming the community's mandate. Recover affected differences, show the scope of support and preserve useful dissent. Keep represented people able to challenge the speaker's account and the claims open to contrary evidence.

### CB.16:7 - Conformance Checklist

For reliance on a collective contribution, establish:

- The receiving decision, authorised recipient and opportunity to affect it are known or their uncertainty is explicit.
- The practical gain and proposed action are supported at the claimed scope, with a serious alternative where it changes the choice.
- Affected positions, meaningful dissent and missing responses remain distinguishable.
- The position is approved and the spokesperson has a valid mandate with usable discretion and return conditions.
- Promised resources and commitments have their actual owners' decisions.
- The response is returned accurately, with the effective result and unfinished work.
- Misrepresentation, new conditions and expired authority can reopen the affected contribution.

A recurring exclusion or an external invitation is enough to recognise the opportunity. It does not supply the authority or evidence required for reliance.

### CB.16:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

| Failure in practice | Repair |
| --- | --- |
| Ask for recognition without a contribution the recipient can assess. | Explain the receiving work, proposed change, benefit, cost and needed support. |
| Treat the most visible members as the whole constituency. | Recover affected positions and state the actual representation scope. |
| Wait for unanimity while hiding the alternatives. | Use the applicable decision rule and carry meaningful disagreement explicitly. |
| Give a speaker an unlimited mandate because they know the subject. | Separate expertise from representation and bound negotiable commitments. |
| Promise other people's time in order to obtain approval. | Request and obtain the actual allocation before relying on the promise. |
| Count access to a meeting as a changed practice. | Return the specific decision and observe whether its conditions and contribution become effective. |
| Report only the favourable response to members. | Include refusals, changed terms, unsupported conditions and needed decisions. |
| Extend one episode's authority into permanent representation. | Obtain a current continuing mandate with returns and replacement. |

### CB.16:9 - Consequences

The community can make a contribution that a decision-maker can act on while keeping its members' positions and authority visible. A representative can negotiate useful details and return a changed question without inventing consent.

The work takes time to recover positions, prepare a feasible request and obtain the return. It may expose differences that prevent a single position. A narrower attributed contribution or an explicit refusal can be more useful than apparent unanimity.

### CB.16:10 - Rationale

A collective voice gains practical value through the work it helps change and the constituency it can legitimately represent. Evidence, mandate and receiving authority answer different questions. Keeping them distinct lets a technically strong proposal remain advice when authority is absent, or an authorised position remain uncertain where evidence is weak.

The return completes the connection. Without it, participants cannot distinguish influence from visibility, correct a misrepresentation or decide whether the effort remains worthwhile. Bounded discretion lets a representative act between meetings while members retain the ability to revise or withdraw the mandate.

### CB.16:11 - SoTA-Echoing

The practice question is how a community can make its expertise and shared interests count in another party's decision. The selected line joins an actionable contribution, a position that preserves differences, a valid mandate and a returned answer. Personal expert comment remains sufficient when no collective representation is needed.

| Source or developed treatment | Choice and effect in this pattern | Limit and accepted cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Etienne Wenger-Trayner, Beverly Wenger-Trayner, Phil Reid and Claude Bruderlein, *Communities of practice within and across organizations*, second edition (2023), pp.112–115 and 179. | **Adapt** stewardship of a domain and a joint response in :4.1–4.3. Preserve disagreement while articulating the professional contribution a decision could use. | Reputation and a learning opportunity do not establish representation authority. Recovering positions and obtaining a mandate add effort to the source's joint-response form. |
| STR.5:4 and LDR.1:4.4. | **Adopt** contribution, recipient, support and alternatives, then use a prepared working conversation. :4.1/:4.3/:4.5 makes the request actionable and handles a changed proposal. | A strategic proposal remains conditional where provision is missing; conversation does not make the recipient's decision. |
| CB.13:4, compared with an informal spokesperson arrangement. | **Adopt** actual mandate, bounded discretion and reconsideration in :4.4/:4.6. **Reject** inferring community authority from expertise, visibility or an invitation. | The scope must fit the real constituency. A smaller attributed contribution is available when the broader mandate cannot be obtained. |

The Guidebook contribution is an analytical adaptation with attribution to its authors, under [CC BY-NC 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/); see the [source text](https://www.wenger-trayner.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/24-02-21-CoP-guidebook-second-edition-final-2.pdf). The constructed cases and mandate connections are developed here.

Reopen the selected approach when the receiving decision changes, a missing constituency invalidates the representation claim, evidence changes the useful contribution, or the burden of obtaining and maintaining the voice exceeds its practical use.

### CB.16:12 - Relations

- **CB.1** recovers the need and participants; **CB.5/14** supplies the relevant expert or method contribution. **CB.6** recognises a contribution but does not establish a collective voice.
- **CB.13** supplies the common decision arrangement and representation mandate. **CB.15** connects different communities when they need a shared response.
- [STR.5:4](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/STRATEGY-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#str54---solution) develops the worthwhile contribution and supporting conditions.
- [LDR.1:4.4](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/LEADERSHIP-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#ldr144---perform-the-smallest-sufficient-working-conversation) supplies preparation and the working exchange. [OCE.14 (OCE.14:4)](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/ORGANIZATION-CHANGE-ENGINEERING-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#oce144---solution) revises an existing arrangement; [OCE.6](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/ORGANIZATION-CHANGE-ENGINEERING-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#oce6---establish-holder-assignments-and-enabling-relations-for-organization-change) obtains assignments and enabling conditions.
- **CB.10** connects observed influence and practical results; **CB.11** revisits continuing provision. **HCD** supplies any later learning contribution.
- **RMP** supplies a needed research result where a consequential claim remains unresolved; a representation mandate does not settle that evidence question.

### CB.16:End

# Applications

These constructed applications show how the language can produce different useful results. The observations and outcomes are stipulated to make the choices inspectable. They do not report field tests or estimate an intervention's effect. Each application can be entered through the direct patterns it names.

## CB.Application:1 - Application 1 - Obtain useful professional help and develop what recurs

Twenty independent repairers sometimes encounter unfamiliar faults. Three initial accounts reveal different difficulties: locating an approved procedure, interpreting an unusual observation and obtaining restricted equipment data. A manufacturer offers a branded forum. Through [CB.1](#cb1---choose-a-useful-cultural-or-community-contribution), the organiser compares a maintained reference, an accountable specialist service and a voluntary case exchange. The data restriction needs its actual owner's decision. The first offer combines a reference route with a brand-neutral, non-urgent case exchange; the sponsor accepts discussion of competing equipment and receives no private case data.

For the first exchange, the case owner supplies permitted observations and a precise question. One qualified peer accepts the task; another initially interested person cannot attend. Under [CB.2](#cb2---arrange-the-first-useful-exchanges), the organiser confirms the first peer's relevant competence and a forty-five-minute window, helps the owner remove confidential material, and tells them what the exchange can promise. The room and conversation chosen through CB.4 let both examine the same permitted material. The owner needs to choose the applicable diagnostic check from an established professional procedure.

The procedure distinguishes a warning at start-up from one reported after normal operation, but the shared account omits when the warning occurred. The peer asks the owner to recover that condition from a permitted record. At the next opportunity, the owner finds that the warning followed normal operation. The peer points to the corresponding part of the procedure. The owner subsequently reports that they could select the next diagnostic check without disclosing restricted data. That is the useful result of this exchange. It establishes neither repair completion nor a general improvement in repair speed.

The organiser records ninety minutes of their own preparation and follow-up, in addition to the peer's time. With CB.7 and CB.9, the association compares repeating that support, paying for preparation or reducing the offer. It chooses one prepared case every two weeks. A capable backup host agrees to cover one absence and rehearses obtaining the permitted material and opening the exchange. An urgent case receives the specialist-service route. CB.3 gives newcomers a small first action—bring one permitted question with the necessary context—and lets others read the later explanation without contributing a case. Under CB.6, the association gives the helper the private acknowledgement they prefer.

A recurring missing condition appears in three later accounts. With [CB.14](#cb14---develop-and-maintain-a-shared-repertoire-of-practice), the repairers decide to make a short preparation aid from the already adequate diagnostic method. A capable practitioner writes it, another checks its conditions, and a new case owner uses it on a contrasting equipment context. That owner can prepare the discriminating material, but a reference is unclear. The maintainer corrects the reference before the aid is offered for wider use. This is a bounded description and use trial. If the underlying diagnostic method had been unsettled, Core Method-development patterns and RMP work would have remained necessary.

The association then visits a maintenance team to compare how cases are prepared. Using [CB.15](#cb15---connect-practices-through-a-useful-joint-contribution), the visitors agree a question with the team and obtain permission to inspect how a real handover is prepared. “Complete handover” means different things in the two settings: the team includes access to an internal history; independent repairers do not have it. The visitors add a preparation question: can the recipient obtain the history used in this account? One repairer uses it to discover missing access before promising the next check. Transferring the team's fuller arrangement would still require that access.

Five repairers want the manufacturer to provide a permitted diagnostic-data route. They compare their needs and remaining differences and authorise a named person to present that five-person request through CB.13 and [CB.16](#cb16---form-and-carry-a-collective-voice-into-a-decision). The representative presents concrete affected work, an access proposal and its restrictions. The manufacturer authorises a limited read-only route for one equipment family. The representative returns the answer and application instructions. Two of the five obtain access for that family; the other three still need data for different equipment. The five decide individually whether the result helps. Expertise supplied a useful contribution; the mandate supplied the right to represent this group; the manufacturer made the access decision.

Finally, CB.10 compares concrete uses, failures, potential later uses and burden. The association retains the low-frequency exchange and preparation aid because the repairers who returned accounts find the next action useful at the agreed cost. It does not claim that attendance, gratitude or three favourable accounts establish a causal business return. If the actual decision later depends on that stronger claim, a suitable inquiry becomes additional work.

## CB.Application:2 - Application 2 - Keep a voluntary garden workable through conflict and succession

Twelve neighbours use a shared garden. They value company, access to growing space and occasional shared produce, but do not want the same frequency or kind of participation. The founder has been hosting two sessions a week and will leave in four weeks. A dispute over the shared tools has also made two newcomers reluctant to return.

[CB.11](#cb11---continue-change-transfer-or-end-a-community-arrangement) begins with what people still want to obtain. The neighbours compare two sessions, one weekly session, independent bed work with limited common upkeep and a seasonal pause. The founder's five hours of weekly organising will disappear. One volunteer offers two hours and another offers one. Their schedules overlap for the novice's half-hour of tool help. Under CB.9, they separate hosting and preparation from money: a small donation can pay consumables but cannot supply absent supervision. One session needs ninety minutes of hosting, thirty minutes of preparation and thirty minutes of qualified tool help: two and a half person-hours in total, leaving half an hour for follow-up. Two sessions remain unsupported.

The group has used the garden by the landowner's permission. CB.13 distinguishes that permission from the neighbours' own decisions. The landowner confirms access for the proposed season and names the conditions that the group cannot alter. The neighbours agree one Saturday session, book shared tools for a stated time and return them to the labelled rack. The host can settle competing requests by first confirmed booking; someone uninvolved hears a challenge. Each user returns a clean tool, and the hosts arrange the common check. People who only work their own beds accept these resource terms without promising to host. The mandate covers common access, use and upkeep.

CB.8 addresses the tool incident separately from the agreement about shared decisions. The people concerned give their accounts to someone not involved in the disputed response. The reviewer finds that the posted return location was obsolete and that a newcomer was blamed for following it. The group corrects the location and the response, and explains the change to those affected. The newcomer can return without accepting a hosting duty. At the next session, two people need the same fork. The host applies the booking rule: the first user returns it after thirty minutes, while the other begins a task using a different tool.

Under CB.7, the two volunteers practise opening the shed, preparing a small task and closing the session with the outgoing organiser. One can host but initially cannot obtain the key on the needed day. The owner supplies a permitted key arrangement before the first receiving session. The new host then runs the shorter session, with the second volunteer, who knows the tool and can supervise its use, helping a novice during the allocated half-hour. When that helper will be absent, the host selects a task within the available capability instead of asking unprepared participants to substitute.

CB.3 makes the first newcomer action visible: meet the named host, choose the prepared task, and ask for help at the stated point. CB.4 supplies a working layout with the right tools and a quiet place to pause. CB.12 adds a reminder chosen by the people who want the weekly activity; occasional participants retain the simpler one-time invitation. CB.6 thanks organisers in their preferred way and supplies promised consumables without converting gratitude into an unpaid commitment.

The first independent session finishes within the available time but reveals fifteen minutes of unbudgeted tool checking. The volunteers use part of the half-hour allowance and agree who will perform it; any further increase reopens the one-session promise. Using CB.10, the group collects short accounts from the host, a newcomer and someone who chose independent bed work. The host's account reveals the tool-checking burden. The independent grower needs to book a tool outside the session; the group supplies a reachable booking contact. These returns change workload and access while preserving different ways to participate.

The transfer under CB.11 includes the usable key arrangement, remaining supplies, current contact and the receiving session's result. The founder's support ends at the agreed date. One unresolved reimbursement has a named receiver after departure. If the landowner withdraws access or neither host can continue, the group returns to the feasible alternatives; a hopeful roster would not justify keeping the promise. The common activity can shrink or end while the neighbours retain what they learned and any independent relationships they choose.

## CB.Application:3 - Application 3 - Extend a practice without a discussion group

A professional association wants more independent repairers to recognise a well-understood fault condition. An adequate method, correctness criteria and authorised examples already exist. [CB.1](#cb1---choose-a-useful-cultural-or-community-contribution) compares a discussion group with making that practice obtainable in individual workshops. The latter fits the receiving situation: people need to choose and perform the action when it arises, without a recurring meeting obligation.

The association obtains a clear explanation, demonstration and representative practice through the relevant HCD contributions. In this case, the approved procedure distinguishes a warning at start-up from one after normal operation. The demonstration shows how the permitted event record determines which check to select. Practice changes the equipment example while retaining that distinction. The learner must select the applicable check and identify the record supporting the choice. A qualified provider checks both against the procedure and gives feedback on the missed condition. Learning-product work supplies a readable guide and corrections, while the provider arranges the information and tools needed for performance.

One learner selects the method correctly but cannot access the required equipment information in their workshop. More reminders or discussion cannot repair this condition. The association obtains a permitted data route from the owner. With access supplied, the learner selects the applicable check from a changed example without a prompt. Another learner needs a reminder to inspect when the warning occurred; the provider retains supported use and prepares further practice instead of recording independent capability prematurely.

C.36 distinguishes obtaining the practice, performing it, continuing to use it and selecting or adapting it under changed conditions. The association therefore looks for particular uses and returns, including an occasion when the method did not fit. Through CB.10 it asks a proportionate follow-up question and uses a failed reference lookup to correct the guide. It does not infer cultural retention from downloads or stable independent performance from one supported attempt.

No communication among the learners is required for these results. If unusual cases later need mutual interpretation, CB.2 becomes a serious additional option. If a newcomer wants occasional company, a voluntary activity can serve that separate purpose. If the professional method itself fails in a changed equipment context, Core Method-development patterns and RMP work becomes current; enlarging the learner population would not resolve that question.

Later, the association replaces the website hosting the guide. Using CB.11, it obtains permission to move the material and a capable person who accepts correction requests. It updates the directory links it controls and notifies existing users through their usual information channel. After the old host closes, an independent user follows the updated directory, reaches the moved guide and reports a missing example reference; the new maintainer restores it. The practice remains obtainable through this provision.

## CB.Application:4 - Application 4 - Separate customer help, learning and provider commitments

A software provider invites customers to exchange examples. Its commercial team hopes to retain subscriptions; participants want to complete particular tasks. Using CB.1, the organiser makes both interests visible and compares peer help, documentation and paid support. An outage requiring a dependable response goes to the provider's service. One customer's non-urgent question fits an exchange: how to send each project team a weekly digest containing only its own records.

Through CB.5, the organiser prepares a short case clinic with a capable contributor and synthetic project data. The contributor proposes a filter and a recipient rule from the product's documented method. The customer tests two projects and discovers that the copied filter still names the first project. They correct it, repeat the test and obtain separate digests for the intended recipients. They return that specific result; actual production use still requires their applicable checks and permission.

Under CB.9, the provider assigns a qualified employee to the thirty-minute clinic every other week and supplies the moderator's preparation time. Volunteers choose whether to contribute examples. The provider obtains a separate agreement before treating an occasional contribution as scheduled production work.

The customer then wants to construct these configurations independently. With the HCD methods, the learning provider supplies a changed task, practice and feedback. The task changes project and recipient conditions; the learner must select and justify the filter and identify missing input. One attempt succeeds with a hint, so the provider arranges another attempt before judging independent performance. The earlier clinic answer remains useful help, while this work addresses the person's capability.

Using CB.10, the organiser follows the separate returns. The customer's report leads to a template that makes the project-specific field explicit. The learning provider uses the observed attempts for its bounded capability judgement. A later commercial inquiry would need suitable grounds to explain subscription retention; clinic activity and favourable stories alone do not settle that explanation.

A sales colleague quotes the customer's contribution as an endorsement without agreement. Through CB.8, the moderator receives the objection, checks the publication with those involved, obtains removal from the responsible publisher and tells the customer what was corrected. The provider clarifies the permitted use of later contributions. The incident concerns the accepted terms of participation, even though the configuration help was useful.

Continue the group under terms participants can understand and accept. Obtain a dependable support service through its responsible provider. A proposed course whose complete programme or qualified provision is still missing remains a proposal; this clinic can contribute worked material without supplying that whole product.

## CB.Application:5 - Connect an external development community with independent workplaces

This is a constructed illustration; its working conditions are stipulated.

A voluntary community brings together practitioners who want to become better at noticing limitations, constructing worthwhile problems and developing usable ways. Some are employees, some independent professionals. The community has capable development contributors but does not claim mastery of every participant's profession. It offers a shared repertoire and a bounded case exchange; a separate paid service can promise individual support under its own terms.

Use [CB.1](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb1---choose-a-useful-cultural-or-community-contribution) to ask what each route should supply. A participant with a settled question may need only the existing explanation. Another wants a qualified specialist answer that the peer exchange cannot promise. A third wants help forming a next problem after a successful transition. Direct them to the contribution they need, including an external subject provider where necessary. Membership is not a condition for using a public resource.

For a first shared undertaking, two participants offer permitted contrasting cases about obtaining and interpreting expert advice. Use [CB.15](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb15---connect-practices-through-a-useful-joint-contribution) to agree the joint work and useful return to each practice. Through [CB.13](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb13---establish-a-workable-mandate-for-shared-decisions), the participants give a small organising group a mandate for this activity and its shared resource; that mandate does not let the group commit their employers or speak for all practitioners. Use [CB.9](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb9---provide-for-community-work-and-agree-its-terms) to obtain the contributors' time for preparation, participation and follow-up. A promised response that exceeds willing capacity must be narrowed or separately provided.

During the exchange, one participant reconstructs why a specialist's conclusion applied to one configuration and not another. A second participant needs further subject knowledge. The community returns that bounded question to a competent provider. Another participant understands the distinction but needs practice applying it under pressure; the human-development contribution through [HCD.6](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Human%20Capability%20Engineering%20DPF%20Suite/HUMAN-CAPABILITY-DEVELOPMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#hcd6---design-representative-practice-tasks) and [HCD.9](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Human%20Capability%20Engineering%20DPF%20Suite/HUMAN-CAPABILITY-DEVELOPMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#hcd9---perform-deliberate-practice-with-feedback) remains separate from the intellectual answer.

Use [CB.14](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb14---develop-and-maintain-a-shared-repertoire-of-practice) to develop a reusable explanation from the cases, preserving the consequential differences and permissions. A qualified AI contribution can help recover sources or construct examples, with the required subject judgement and checks supplied by the actual arrangement. A further practitioner uses the explanation in a different permitted case, following [C.36.MC's reconstruction and adaptation (FPF C.36.MC:4.5)](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/FPF-Spec.md#c36mc45---make-a-practice-recoverable-and-changeable-by-its-recipients). Observe which operation that practitioner performs and which help remains necessary. That result can support a bounded reconstruction or use claim; publication and attendance alone cannot.

After this useful result, the community notices a harder problem: can another organiser help participants form worthwhile questions without the founder choosing each one? [FPF C.40.NP](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/FPF-Spec.md#c40np---continue-from-a-result-to-new-attainable-problems) supplies the continuation. Use [CB.7](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb7---prepare-and-sustain-distributed-organising) to prepare a willing successor around an actual episode. When the successor needs to develop an ability, use the learning contribution through [HCD.6](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Human%20Capability%20Engineering%20DPF%20Suite/HUMAN-CAPABILITY-DEVELOPMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#hcd6---design-representative-practice-tasks) and [HCD.9](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Human%20Capability%20Engineering%20DPF%20Suite/HUMAN-CAPABILITY-DEVELOPMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#hcd9---perform-deliberate-practice-with-feedback); the community must also obtain the required time, access and qualified help with unresolved subject questions. The new organiser's performance, the participants' development and the repertoire contribution remain different results.

An employer may separately invite the community to support development at its workplaces. The agreement must connect the community's contribution with the employer's actual work opportunities and decision rights through [OCE.18](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/ORGANIZATION-CHANGE-ENGINEERING-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#oce18---arrange-capability-development-and-receiving-work-in-an-organizational-transition) and [LDR.2](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/LEADERSHIP-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#ldr2---agree-feasible-joint-contributions). Funding alone does not supply permission to use confidential learning material in identifiable personnel reports. Stop the activity that depends on missing permission; independently useful public guidance can remain available.

The community can remain a specialised development provider with outside professional suppliers. It can also obtain shared administration or learning infrastructure from a common service. If nobody can maintain the promised repertoire or response service, use the [continuation and withdrawal question in CB.11](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md#cb11---continue-change-transfer-or-end-a-community-arrangement) to obtain a successor, reduce the promise or end it while settling accepted commitments.

## CB.Application:End



# Community Management Principles Framework Sources and Edition Notes

## CB.Sources:1 - Source use and limits

The sources below shaped the connected language. Their practical contributions, evidence and limits remain distinct. The detailed comparisons in each pattern's SoTA-Echoing section should be used when a source-specific choice matters.

| Source family | Contribution retained in this edition | Boundary, alternative and return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| David Spinks, *The Business of Belonging* (2021) | A purposeful offer, manual early organising, workable participation, recognition, organising support, provision and accounts of value. These inform CB.1–12. | Treat numerical anecdotes and company examples as historical source accounts. Growth, commercial retention and visible activity do not define every useful contribution. Compare resources, services and smaller voluntary arrangements against the actual need. |
| Etienne Wenger-Trayner, Beverly Wenger-Trayner, Phil Reid and Claude Bruderlein, *Communities of practice within and across organizations*, second edition (2023) | Positive forms of learning through practice, activities and relationships, shared repertoire, reciprocal comparison, boundary work, collective stewardship, value inquiry and renewal. Temporary participant groups also supply shared observation and support. These contributions inform the corresponding methods, especially CB.4/5/7/10/11/14–16. | Use these forms when joint participation helps. Their community-of-practice focus does not require communication for every wider cultural purpose. Treat development dimensions as optional, and use C.28/RMP for a question that depends on causal explanation. |
| Community Canvas Guidebook (2017) | Historical organising questions about common decisions, mandate, mixed local and common responsibility, and conflicts involving decision-makers, developed in CB.8/13. | An informal repertoire supplies options. The actual arrangement needs a valid mandate, feasible operations and correction; a new body is unnecessary where an adequate owner can decide. |
| Core Protocols, linked in CB.13:4.5.1 | A connected decision option for an adopting small team. | Its participation obligations need explicit acceptance; this is not the default governance of a voluntary community. |
| A. Levenchuk's community ontology and systemicity essays (September 2024), read with C.36 | Cultural contribution can develop carriers of a practice without a communicating collective or one collective agent. CB.1 and the independent-use branch make that choice practical. | A conceptual distinction does not establish the effectiveness of an intervention. Obtain the method, learning, provision and use observations that the selected contribution needs. |
| A. Levenchuk, [role communities inside the company](https://ailev.ru/1741032.html) and [role communities around the company](https://ailev.ru/1741983.html), November 2024 | Distinguish an organization, its employee community, external participant communities and populations carrying a practice; preserve participant purposes and the real work transferred to them. These distinctions clarify the field boundary and its organizational and provider relations. | These are conceptual proposals. They do not establish that every enterprise needs an office, that informal participation removes cost, or that one provider can direct the whole recipient organization. |
| Research and practitioner reports used by individual patterns | Work on participation rules, appeals, context and repeated action qualifies the mechanisms and evidence in CB.8/12/13. The Duolingo contributor-programme announcement gives a historical account of changed production conditions in CB.9. | Retain the actual population, observations and limitations. Moderator reports, written rules, self-reported habits and an organisation's explanation answer different questions from experienced fairness, automatic performance or causal effectiveness. Follow each body's exact source and comparison. |
| FPF Core and the domain suppliers below | Cultural distinctions, useful-contribution comparison, actual work arrangements, learning provision, professional-method development, evidence, capacity and resource reasoning. | Reuse the needed substantive result. A reference alone does not obtain qualified work, authority, access or an operating service. |

Source returns: [The Business of Belonging](https://www.wiley-vch.de/en/areas-interest/finance-economics-law/the-business-of-belonging-978-1-119-76612-4); [Communities of practice guidebook, second edition](https://www.wenger-trayner.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/24-02-21-CoP-guidebook-second-edition-final-2.pdf); [Community Canvas](https://github.com/communitycanvas/documents/blob/master/CommunityCanvas-Guidebook.pdf); [community ontology](https://ailev.livejournal.com/1735885.html); [systemicity discussion](https://ailev.livejournal.com/1736164.html).

The Guidebook adaptations are attributed to its four authors and retain [CC BY-NC 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) as identified in the affected patterns. The constructed cases and connections are developed here. Other third-party contributions retain the terms and qualifications stated at their source returns. The edition's original content has the separate licence stated in [Edition and use](#edition-and-use).

The [Architectural Reference](#community-management-principles-framework-architectural-reference) explains the connected language and the consequences of these sources for its use.

## CB.Sources:End


# Edition and use

## CB.Edition:1 - Edition and citation

**Community Management — Participation and practice-support edition, 12 October 2026.** Full-text home: [Community Management Principles Framework](https://github.com/ailev/FPF/blob/main/DPFs/Management%20DPF%20Suite/COMMUNITY-MANAGEMENT-PRINCIPLES-FRAMEWORK.md).

This edition contains the sixteen complete CB pattern bodies, its Readme and Architectural Reference, the constructed applications, source-use account and supplier returns. It is written for people and assisting agents constructing or changing community participation and its contributions under the conditions each Method states. The retained independent-use application shows a qualified alternative to community formation, not a promise to contain every cultural Method. It does not promise a complete professional method, learning product, commercial strategy or research programme for every activity a community undertakes.

CB is this framework's reference code; a local numeric locator completes each PatternID, such as CB.14. When citing this publication outside the framework, name Community Management and identify this edition and the particular revision when its text matters. Authority to act and evidence for an intervention's effect depend on the particular use and its grounds.

## CB.Edition:2 - Product-series rule

The **Community Management Principles Framework** product series collects editions for community organisers, participants, practitioners, sponsors and assisting agents who construct, conduct, support and renew useful participation and joint contributions. A product-constitution decision begins this collection by admitting the **Participation and practice-support edition** above as its first edition. Publication and Suite inclusion are separate acts.

Select Methods for offer and exchange, participation and activity, distributed organising, rules and mandates, provision, value, continuation, repertoire work and boundary representation. Admit only complete editions whose independent practical use and required direct suppliers have been qualified. Preserve a sufficient individual or provider alternative, unequal authority and cultural continuation outside community participation. The edition must explain the useful results it supplies and return to obtainable external Methods for stronger or different claims.

Later editions may refine, add, split or redistribute Methods while preserving that participation-and-contribution promise, independent bounded use, practical receiving results and supplier boundaries. Admission requires a supported edition relation to the actual source edition (`EpistemeEditionRelation`), satisfaction of these rules and an effective admission decision. This applies also to a predecessor edition, fork, translation or other derivative. Replacing those identity anchors with another governed practice requires another product series. A different title, publication home, Suite membership or maintenance arrangement alone does not replace them.

Loss of a necessary use, defeated source grounds or a broken direct return requires review of the affected qualification and a decision to repair, correct an unsupported admission claim or retire the affected offering. An admitted edition remains a historical member while this series continues, including when superseded, unavailable or retired. Explicit retirement of the series ends the collection and current belonging while preserving the historical facts; later active use requires a new constitution. A maintaining party, maintenance commitment, future edition or continued availability requires its own grounds.

## CB.Edition:3 - Attribution and use

Original framework content: Anatoly Levenchuk, with AI-assisted development and review. Original content is offered under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Third-party material and adaptations retain their own terms as identified above and in each pattern. Preserve applicable attribution and source boundaries when copying or adapting a standalone publication.

## CB.Edition:End

# Corporate Finance Readme

## Practical entries

The connected cases below follow a financial question through the results it needs: dated cash into funding and execution, the value of an acquired interest into a transaction comparison, and a changed receipt into a treasury response. Enter where the missing result lies and reuse adequate supplied accounts. The short project-value example at the end also shows where a direct calculation can finish.

These are constructed examples, not market offers or a required sequence. Use the Table of Contents for a known PatternID or another financial question. When working with a colleague or assistant, describe the payment, investment or exposure and the answer you need in ordinary language.

### FIN-E1 - A profitable order leaves a day-7 cash gap

- **Situation:** An operating account establishes that an order is feasible and brings 1,200 on day 28 against incremental payments of 440 on day 0 and 100 on day 7. The whole-business baseline, after all other flows, has cash of 500 at each relevant date.
- **Question:** Which available arrangement funds the order while preserving the required cash?
- **First useful result or blocker:** The liquidity calculation finds a day-7 gap of 40 before any positive reserve. A response is usable only if its money arrives in time and its later payments remain fundable.
- **Start with:** [FIN.2](#fin2---assess-liquidity-and-funding-needs-by-date) for the dated cash account, then [FIN.3](#fin3---manage-working-capital-and-cash-conversion) for the customer-advance alternative or [FIN.10](#fin10---design-financing-instruments-and-terms) for financing terms. Use [FIN.15](#fin15---execute-treasury-and-liquidity-decisions) for the selected permitted action.
- **Stop or return:** Complete the comparison with a supported choice of an arrangement whose receipts are available in time and whose repayments are fundable, or identify the specific missing condition. Return when collection, reserve, fees, draw access or repayment changes.

The order requires 26–29 rig-hours. The supplied operating plan has 20 usable hours plus an available ten-hour block costing 240. Materials cost 200 and supplier service costs 100. Materials and the block require 440 on day 0; the supplier's 100 is due on day 7. Those adequate operating and accounting results give the 540 of incremental payments and a favorable contribution of 660. Finance can use them directly.

After paying 440, cash is 60. The day-7 payment of 100 creates the gap of 40. A committed facility can supply up to 80 before that payment; it withholds a fee of 3 and requires principal plus interest of 2 on day 28. A gross draw of 43 supplies net cash 40. Alternatively, the customer has agreed to pay 96 on day 6 against 100 of the invoice, leaving 1,100 on day 28.

| Available arrangement | Cash after day-7 payment | Cash after day-28 flows | Incremental gain over the 500 baseline |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Draw 43, then repay 45 | 0 | 1,155 | 655 |
| Receive the agreed advance of 96 | 56 | 1,156 | 656 |

On these conditions, the advance provides one more unit of gain and a larger buffer. Without the customer's agreement, the proposed advance is not available to pay the day-7 obligation. If a positive reserve is required, the zero-cash facility row must change. If collection moves to day 40 but the loan remains due on day 28, its 45 repayment becomes a new gap. A positive total contribution does not establish an extension.

[FIN.16](#fin16---prepare-a-finance-recommendation-and-return-it-for-a-decision) uses the funded alternatives and their operating conditions to return the advance recommendation, or conditional advice if agreement or draw access is missing. Treasury then uses [FIN.15](#fin15---execute-treasury-and-liquidity-decisions) under the existing authority to perform the selected action and reconcile what actually settled. If the collection expectation moves to day 40, [FIN.17](#fin17---refresh-financial-models-and-data) updates the liquidity projection and returns the unfunded day-28 repayment to [FIN.10](#fin10---design-financing-instruments-and-terms). The operating contribution can remain 660 on unchanged operating grounds, but the earlier net gain of 655 must be recalculated with a feasible repayment arrangement and its cost.

### FIN-TRANSACTION - Compare an acquisition price with value and available funding

- **Situation:** An operating business is valued at 100, and the buyer is considering paying 100 for its equity.
- **Question:** What value would the buyer obtain at the proposed price, and can the purchase be funded on that basis?
- **First useful result or blocker:** A transaction comparison that includes the acquired claims and buyer's incremental effects, with the funding condition still needed for action.
- **Start with:** [FIN.7](#fin7---value-assets-and-the-corporation) if the value of the acquired interest is unresolved; [FIN.9](#fin9---compare-capital-investments-and-allocations) if that value is already supplied.
- **Stop or return:** A supported conditional recommendation can finish the advice. Return to the affected value or funding calculation when price, included claims, benefits or payment conditions change.

In FIN.7's constructed case, operating enterprise value is 100. Debt with market value 30 remains in the acquired company, and included excess cash of 10 is freely transferable after closing. With no other claim adjustment, standalone equity value is 100 − 30 + 10 = 80. That is the interest value FIN.9 uses to compare with the equity price.

The buyer-specific benefits have present value 30, while integration and other incremental costs have present value 15, on the same date, currency and after-tax basis. At price 100, buyer value is 80 + 30 − 15 − 100 = −5. At price 90, it is +5.
The +5 is a conditional financial result. [FIN.2](#fin2---assess-liquidity-and-funding-needs-by-date) uses the purchase payments and their dates in the buyer's cash account. The acquired cash of 10 becomes available after closing and cannot fund a payment due before then. If the buyer needs external funds, [FIN.10](#fin10---design-financing-instruments-and-terms) compares obtainable terms by net proceeds, availability and later payments. A material change to debt and equity mix calls for [FIN.11](#fin11---select-capital-structure); a relied-on borrowing restriction calls for [FIN.12](#fin12---preserve-covenant-headroom-and-financing-flexibility). These results can change whether the purchase is available and what financing effects enter the valuation. Count any such effect once on a matching basis.

[FIN.16](#fin16---prepare-a-finance-recommendation-and-return-it-for-a-decision) combines the value comparison with those funding results for the buyer's decision. It can return a price-conditioned recommendation or the funding condition preventing action. If the expected benefits change, [FIN.17](#fin17---refresh-financial-models-and-data) returns their consequences to FIN.9; if the acquired debt or cash differs from the valued interest, return to FIN.7 before retaining the +5 conclusion. Using the recommendation for action still depends on the assumed consents and ability to realize benefits. When the buyer must compare the acquisition with a capital project and a paid expansion right, use the [connected capital-use example in FIN.9](#fin951---a-project-an-acquisition-and-an-expansion-choice). It constructs the values and feasible combinations at one date.

### FIN-E3 - A currency hedge meets a partial customer payment

- **Situation:** A customer owes 100 foreign units on day 30. A physical forward requires delivery of 100 foreign units for 90 home units that day, but the customer pays only 60.
- **Question:** What does the hedge protect, and what must treasury now fund?
- **First useful result or blocker:** At spot 0.95 home per foreign unit, buying the missing 40 costs 38 home units. If funded and settled, current net home cash is 52 and the unpaid customer claim of 40 foreign units remains.
- **Start with:** [FIN.14](#fin14---decide-whether-and-how-to-hedge-or-transfer-financial-risk) for the combined receipt and hedge; [FIN.13](#fin13---identify-and-measure-financial-exposures) if the underlying exposure or remaining claim is unclear.
- **Stop or return:** Settle through [FIN.15](#fin15---execute-treasury-and-liquidity-decisions) only with the required funding and authority. Reassess the remaining claim and future protection after actual performance.

With the full customer receipt, the forward exchanges the 100 foreign units for 90 home units. FIN.14's partial-receipt case keeps the customer's outstanding claim separate from the forward's unchanged delivery obligation. The receipt supplies 60, so treasury must obtain the other 40. Buying them at 0.95 requires 38 home units; purchase and forward settlement together give 90 − 38 = 52 of net home cash.

That net amount does not supply the money needed before the currency purchase. [FIN.2](#fin2---assess-liquidity-and-funding-needs-by-date) checks usable funds at that time. In FIN.15's continuation, only 20 home units are usable, leaving a funding need of 18. Treasury needs a funded purchase or must return the execution problem through the provider's supported recovery and the relevant decision authority. Entering a purchase instruction does not establish delivery.

After actual purchase and forward settlement, FIN.15 reconciles the amounts and dates. The unpaid customer claim of 40 remains unless a separate event changes it. [FIN.17](#fin17---refresh-financial-models-and-data) carries the partial payment into the cash and exposure accounts; FIN.13 and FIN.14 use the remaining claim, its expected collection and existing protection to decide whether future protection needs changing.

FIN.15's [funded continuation](#fin1552---complete-the-partial-receipt-hedge-with-actual-interim-finance) makes the remaining steps explicit. With the stated zero reserve, no other flows, 20 opening cash and an attainable draw of 18 before purchase, the currency purchase leaves home cash zero. The forward then supplies 90; repayment of 18.50 leaves 71.50. The net increase of 51.50 is the original contribution 52 less finance cost 0.50, and the customer still owes 40.

Before entering a new hedge, FIN.14's [comparison of fixed and optional protection](#fin1451---compare-a-fixed-amount-a-smaller-amount-and-optional-protection) shows how another collection amount can change the preferred design. That comparison does not cancel the already contracted forward in this entry. A changed exposure returns to the actual rights and available modification terms.

### FIN-E2 - Value a project before arranging its funding

- **Situation:** A project pays 1,000 now and returns 600 at the end of each of two years. These are complete incremental after-tax operating cash flows, with no terminal value.
- **Question:** Does the project add financial value at a matching annual required return of 10%?
- **First useful result or blocker:** FIN.6 gives NPV 41.32 on these grounds. This completes the stated value calculation; it does not provide the initial 1,000.
- **Start with:** FIN.6. Use FIN.5 if the required return is unresolved and FIN.2 if the next question is payment capacity.
- **Stop or return:** Return when cash, timing, risk basis or a competing capital use changes the answer.

# Corporate Finance Principles Framework Architectural Reference

## FIN.Reference:1 - Problem frame

Use this language when a corporate-finance analyst, treasurer, CFO or manager must answer a financial question about the corporation's investments, funding, liquidity, exposures, distributions or recovery. It assumes ordinary familiarity with financial statements, amounts, percentages and dates. Additional mathematical, market or institutional knowledge is stated with the methods that need it. It supplies procedures and worked cases for making financial consequences usable in decisions.

The governed field is corporate finance. Investor portfolio selection, prudential banking, a complete legal or accounting manual and the broader economics of exchange are outside this edition. A formal valuation, tax conclusion, regulated action or legal process uses the actual applicable professional requirements when that claim is needed.

## FIN.Reference:2 - Problem

A corporation can be profitable and unable to pay, buy a valuable business at a destructive price, hedge a currency while retaining collection risk, or improve one financial model while creating incompatible commitments elsewhere. The difficulty is often the connection between valid local calculations and the actual choice they are meant to support.

The language addresses those connections without reducing finance to generic advice about “making better decisions”. Practitioners use the analytical methods to calculate dated cash positions and values, compare financing terms, assess exposures, design protection and prepare recommendations. Treasury methods guide permitted financial actions and verification of their effects.

## FIN.Reference:3 - Forces

Financial work balances value, payment continuity, risk, flexibility, control, evidence and limited attention. It must use actual institutional conditions while remaining small enough for a routine decision. A more complete model can be useful, but only when its distinctions can change action or warranted reliance. Uncertainty can justify a range or conditional recommendation without making every question a new research project.

## FIN.Reference:4 - Solution

Enter through the missing useful result. Cash and account methods are FIN.1–4; value and allocation are FIN.5–9; financing is FIN.10–12; retention and recovery are FIN.21–22; exposure and execution are FIN.13–15; advice and continuing practice are FIN.16–20. The Parts group these contributions for reading. A pattern can be used in several combinations.

When combining results, preserve their material common conditions: corporation and claimant perspective, financial positions, baseline, currency and units, valuation and payment dates, tax and risk treatment, and access to the same money or capacity. Do not count one receipt, benefit or available facility twice. A valid set of local calculations may still fail this joint condition.

The acquisition and divestment profile is a bounded use of FIN.9. FIN.7 supplies the interest's standalone value; FIN.9 adds price, combination or separation effects and the remaining business; FIN.10–12 supply financing conditions where needed. This is a financial transaction comparison, not the whole acquisition process.

An adequate supplied result can be used directly. A finance analyst need not reconstruct operating capacity, create a new semantic model or visit every related pattern before calculating. FIN.16 connects completed results to a receiving decision when a direct result is not already enough.

Also ask what larger work a present operation performs when that connection is unclear. In FIN.2's example, solving for a loan's gross draw performs part of sizing the financing, and that sizing performs part of constructing the dated payment plan. The payer, fee, reserve and availability conditions connect these operations. [FPF B.1.5.EW][EW] helps recover such a connection and identify a constituent operation to learn, obtain or correct. The bank's later transfer and another person's use of the completed forecast have their own relations to this analytical work. Use an already understood connection directly.

## FIN.Reference:5 - Archetypal Grounding

FIN-E1 supplies the whole first-use case. The operating plan and incremental account are already adequate. FIN.2 exposes the gap hidden by the positive contribution; FIN.3 compares an agreed advance with the available loan; the treasurer uses FIN.15 to perform the selected permitted action. When collection moves to day 40, repayment on day 28 becomes unfunded. FIN.17 helps the analyst reconsider the financing recommendation while retaining unaffected operating grounds.

The language also reaches a different result when the financial question changes. FIN.6 calculates positive project NPV without claiming funding. FIN.9's acquisition has equity value 80, additional benefits 30 and costs 15: a price of 100 gives buyer value −5, while 90 gives +5. FIN.22 compares the same expected recovery at different dates. These constructed cases establish how to apply the methods, not evidence of organizational adoption or measured financial improvement.

## FIN.Reference:6 - Bias-Annotation

The corporation is the usual receiving perspective, but its owners, creditors, employees, customers and providers can bear different consequences. Name those interests and applicable constraints when they change the question. Public-company market evidence may not transfer to a private firm; consolidated accounts may not establish local access to cash; one jurisdiction's financing rule may not apply elsewhere.

All numerical cases are constructed and use the expressly stated terms. They are not quotations of current market offers. Use actual current facts for the corporation's real decision.

## FIN.Reference:7 - Conformance Checklist

Can the practitioner identify the receiving action, corporation and claim perspective? Does each method supply its promised financial result on stated grounds? Do combined results preserve the joint conditions in FIN.Reference:4, including payment timing and shared resources? Are institutional facts sufficient for the claimed action, and are unresolved ones specific? Can another practitioner replay the decisive case and identify a condition that changes it? Are recommendation, decision and execution distinguished where the result crosses those boundaries?

Use each pattern's checklist to examine its narrower claim. A completed direct use does not require evidence for every other pattern.

## FIN.Reference:8 - Common Anti-Patterns and How to Avoid Them

Treating profit as cash hides the first-use gap; use FIN.2. Treating enterprise value as an equity purchase price hides claims and consideration; use FIN.7 and FIN.9. Treating a hedge as a customer guarantee hides the partial-receipt branch; use FIN.14. Treating a new template as improved practice hides actual use; use FIN.20.

Another failure is to turn these corrections into a compulsory chain. Start with an adequate existing question and account, and obtain only the missing contribution.

## FIN.Reference:9 - Consequences

The financial result becomes usable at the place where it can change a decision: the dated shortage, value threshold, price, financing condition, residual exposure or actual settlement. The language also permits a supported continuation or a bounded unresolved condition.

The cost is explicit attention to assumptions, dates and effects that a familiar summary can omit. Preserve that detail when it matters; a routine direct result should remain routine.

## FIN.Reference:10 - Architectural Rationale

The language retains domain procedures because a general choice method cannot calculate cash conversion, discount a project or reconcile an instrument's proceeds by itself. It reuses Management Accounting, Financial Domain Modeling and Operations Management for their independently useful results instead of making them three sections of a larger finance prerequisite.

Separate patterns distinguish value, allocation, funding and execution because the same case can obtain one result and fail another. In acquisition and divestment comparisons, FIN.9 combines supplied valuations with the price, transaction effects and financing conditions.
